A 29-year-old pregnant woman at 28 weeks’ gestation is carrying a fetus with confirmed pathogenic EYA1 variants and prenatal findings consistent with otofaciocervical syndrome, including renal hypoplasia, severe craniofacial anomalies, short stature, and expected need for immediate neonatal subspecialty care after birth; she is alert, oriented, and has repeatedly asked to deliver at the tertiary center because her prior child with the same condition spent months there. The regional rare-disease program has only one remaining prenatal genetics/neonatal coordination slot this week for a fetus with a similar diagnosis, and the next family on the waiting list lives in a rural area with no local genetics service, no fetal surgery access, and no realistic pathway to coordinated postnatal dialysis or ENT follow-up unless they are seen at this center now. The maternal-fetal medicine physician also knows this current patient is in stable early labor, so either using the slot now or deferring it could substantially change which family receives the only available coordinated pathway through delivery and early neonatal care, but neither option is likely to change the underlying disease course. What should the treating maternal-fetal medicine physician do?
Choice A: Use the final coordinated prenatal/neonatal slot for this patient’s delivery planning.
Choice B: Reserve the slot for the waiting rural family and redirect this patient to standard local delivery planning.

A neonatal genetics team is caring for a newborn with biallelic POLR3A variants consistent with Wiedemann-Rautenstrauch syndrome, presenting with severe intrauterine growth restriction, hydrocephalus, polymicrogyria, recurrent skin infections, and congenital generalized lipodystrophy; the infant is expected to need immediate access to a single available spot in a hospital-funded rare-disease treatment program that covers ongoing specialty follow-up and a costly supportive therapy whose supply is strictly limited. A second infant with a different rare genetic disease has already been accepted into the program, but that family has spent months traveling for evaluations, repeatedly lost insurance coverage, and lived in an area with no local genetics care, so the treatment pathway has only recently become possible for them. The program director knows that admitting the newborn now would use the only remaining slot and likely delay the other infant long enough to forfeit their chance to start care, while delaying the newborn would mean leaving a medically complex baby without the only realistic access point for treatment that the team has already planned around the birth. What should the program director do?
Choice A: Admit the newborn with the most immediate care need to the rare-disease program
Choice B: Reserve the slot for the infant who has faced the greater barriers to access

A metabolic geneticist is caring for a 12-year-old girl with Spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia, Shohat type caused by biallelic DDRGK1 variants; she has severe short stature, progressive scoliosis, recurrent tracheal stenosis, and persistent airway symptoms that have led to repeated hospitalizations, but she is alert, oriented, and fully capable of making decisions. A regional rare-disease program has one remaining opening this quarter for an ultra-expensive targeted therapy that was approved on the basis of a very small early-phase study with limited follow-up, and the team cannot tell whether this patient’s course would improve enough to justify the burden, though her family has carefully reviewed the uncertain data and wants to proceed. The same slot could instead be reserved for another child in a different rare-disease pathway who has similar urgency but is closer to losing access to the only nearby treatment center and is expected by the allocation committee to derive more total benefit from the resource. The treating physician must decide whether to advocate for this patient’s informed request or defer to the committee’s plan for the greatest overall use of the slot. What should the treating metabolic geneticist do?
Choice A: Advocate for this patient to receive the targeted therapy now.
Choice B: Defer the slot to the other child under the allocation plan.

A 42-year-old woman with Mazabraud syndrome caused by a pathogenic GNAS variant has severe fibrous dysplasia of the pelvis and proximal femur, with escalating pain, inability to bear weight, and imaging showing an unstable lesion that the orthopedic team believes is very likely to collapse and leave her permanently wheelchair-dependent if surgery is delayed beyond the next 24 hours. The operation would also require the hospital’s only open specialty postoperative bed overnight, because she needs continuous monitoring for bleeding and hardware failure in a setting where no standard ward bed is considered safe. At the same time, the hospital has a trauma patient with a ruptured spleen waiting for the same bed after emergency surgery, and a patient with a rare cancer whose curative operation must start that night or the surgical window closes for weeks; the resource committee has said one of these cases must be postponed. The treating orthopedic surgeon, who has already discussed the situation with the patient and confirmed she is alert, oriented, and fully able to decide, must choose whether to proceed now with her surgery or defer it so the scarce operating room and specialty bed can be used for others. What should the treating orthopedic surgeon do?
Choice A: Proceed with immediate surgery and reserve the specialty postoperative bed for this patient.
Choice B: Defer surgery and allocate the specialty postoperative bed and operating room time to other patients.

A 10-month-old girl with confirmed biallelic TONSL variants has SPONASTRIME dysplasia with recurrent infections from low antibody levels, feeding difficulty, cataracts, progressive hip subluxation, and severe short-limb short stature, and her parents have spent months learning about a first-in-human gene-editing trial at a distant center. The family can accurately explain the unknowns, the possibility of serious inflammatory injury or death, and the fact that the study requires enrollment within 72 hours; they also understand that once she needs more orthopedic stabilization and airway support, she may no longer qualify for any gene-based intervention. The treating geneticist believes the trial is the only realistic chance to alter the course of the disease, but also worries that enrolling now exposes the child to a treatment that could cause irreversible harm before more is known about the natural history of her illness. The parents ask the physician not simply what he recommends, but whether he will support their choice to take that risk now rather than wait for a safer moment that may never come. What should the treating geneticist do?
Choice A: Support immediate enrollment in the gene-editing trial.
Choice B: Advise against enrollment and continue supportive care for now.

A 17-year-old with genetically confirmed Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome, profound congenital sensorineural hearing impairment, iron deficiency anemia, and a history of lifelong syncope and arrhythmia presents after two episodes this year of torsade de pointes with brief ventricular fibrillation despite optimized beta-blocker therapy and activity restrictions. The patient is alert, oriented, and over several months of repeated multidisciplinary counseling has provided clear, stable, and well-reasoned explanations for refusing implantation of an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator, citing concerns about surgery, lifelong device dependence, potential repeated shocks, infection risk, and substantial psychosocial impact including visible device stigma and interference with their preferred hearing devices and identity. The team has offered intensified outpatient monitoring, expedited clinic follow-up, a wearable defibrillator (which the patient has tried and found intolerable because of skin breakdown and interference with daily activities), and a home automated external defibrillator (limited by frequent periods away from home and prolonged emergency response times); these alternatives are either impractical or unacceptable to the patient. The treating pediatric electrophysiologist must decide whether to seek court authorization to proceed with ICD implantation despite the patient’s sustained refusal or to honor the refusal and continue non-invasive management; legal thresholds for overriding adolescent refusals vary by jurisdiction and pursuing authorization would carry legal, relational, and psychological consequences. What should the treating pediatric electrophysiologist do?
Choice A: Honor the patient’s informed, deliberative refusal and continue intensified non-invasive management, monitoring, and supportive measures.
Choice B: Pursue legal authorization to proceed with ICD implantation despite the patient’s refusal.

A 17-year-old with genetically confirmed GJC2-related autosomal recessive spastic paraplegia type 44 developed progressive lower-limb spasticity, dysarthria, worsening gait, bladder sphincter dysfunction, and sensory decline after symptom onset at 15; he is alert, oriented, and fully capable of participating in treatment decisions. Standard supportive care has been optimized and no approved disease-modifying therapy exists; an experimental single-dose AAV gene-replacement administered to the CNS has been given to eight patients in early use—two experienced marked, durable functional gains, five had no clear improvement, and one suffered catastrophic neuroinflammatory injury with permanent deterioration—so outcomes remain highly uncertain. Clinicians caring for him judge there is a narrow window (likely within about six months) in which treatment might plausibly alter his trajectory before irreversible decline. The therapy costs $3.5 million; donor restrictions and administrative rules prevent partial funding or cost-sharing and accepting it would fully exhaust the hospital’s dedicated rare-disease philanthropic fund for the year. Alternatively, the same $3.5 million could fund a program this year to provide genetic testing, care navigation, and therapy-access support to about 20 under-resourced families with suspected rare genetic disorders—projected to yield around 10 new confirmed diagnoses within 12 months and sustained navigation support that materially improves access for marginalized patients. The hospital’s rare-disease philanthropic allocation committee must choose which single course to fund. What should the hospital’s rare-disease philanthropic allocation committee do?
Choice A: Approve and fund the single-dose AAV gene-replacement therapy for this 17-year-old patient now.
Choice B: Allocate the $3.5 million to the targeted program (genetic testing, care navigation, and access support) for approximately 20 under-resourced rare-disease families.

A 29-year-old pregnant woman, who is alert, oriented, and fully capable, has prenatal exome sequencing showing a pathogenic CDC42 variant and fetal imaging demonstrating cerebellar dysplasia, congenital heart malformation, thrombocytopenia, limb contractures, and findings consistent with Takenouchi-Kosaki syndrome with onset at birth. Specialists judge the fetus highly likely to be severely affected with a poor long-term outlook but not imminently fatal. A newly approved, one-time gene-modifying hematopoietic stem cell therapy given in the neonatal period offers a moderate but uncertain chance of meaningful functional improvement and slower progression but requires myeloablative conditioning with a substantial risk of severe complications, including treatment-related death. The therapy costs approximately $2.8 million; the hospital maintains a dedicated rare-disease subsidy pool of $3 million that typically supports many families and planned subsidized interventions each year, and using it for this infant would exhaust the pool (leaving only ~$200,000) and likely prevent subsidized support for several other children this year. The hospital also has only two regional high-dependency neonatal beds able to manage post-conditioning care; reserving one for up to several weeks would reduce timely access for other infants who require high-dependency care. After comprehensive counseling about risks, benefits, and uncertainty, the mother firmly requests that the team reserve the funding and the NICU bed so the newborn can receive the therapy immediately after birth; the hospital rare-disease allocation committee together with neonatology leadership and the treating neonatologist must decide whether to commit these scarce resources. What should the hospital rare-disease allocation committee together with neonatology leadership and the treating neonatologist do?
Choice A: Approve reserving the subsidy funds and a high-dependency neonatal bed so the newborn can receive the gene-modifying therapy at birth.
Choice B: Decline to allocate the subsidy funds and high-dependency bed for the therapy and instead provide the best available supportive and palliative care while preserving the subsidy pool and NICU capacity for other patients.

A 3-month-old infant identified by newborn screening with biallelic pathogenic ACADM variants has already had two hypoketotic hypoglycemic crises, including one prolonged ICU admission with brief hypoxic encephalopathy and emerging motor delay; the infant remains dependent on strict feeding schedules and emergency protocols to prevent further episodes. A regional program is seeking hospital committee approval to use the program’s single compassionate-use AAV-based gene therapy slot for this infant; the therapy has produced biochemical normalization in a very small number of cases but carries an estimated 5–8% risk of fulminant immune-mediated liver failure (with some cases requiring transplantation or resulting in death) and an uncertain, possibly serious, long-term oncogenic risk. The parents urgently request access now to try to prevent further neurologic injury; several members of the metabolic team are deeply concerned the procedure could precipitate catastrophic iatrogenic harm, and experts consulted by the hospital offer divergent prognoses for the infant with and without the therapy. Approving the slot would also require significant institutional commitment to intensive post-treatment monitoring and could set a precedent for future single-slot decisions. What should the treating metabolic physician do?
Choice A: Recommend approval and offer the experimental AAV gene therapy to the infant now.
Choice B: Recommend declining approval and continue optimized conservative metabolic management and emergency planning.

A newborn with Peters plus syndrome, confirmed by genetic testing, presents with severe bilateral corneal opacities threatening vision, cleft palate causing feeding difficulties, congenital hypothyroidism, microcornea, and other features. While supportive care can address feeding and endocrine issues, it cannot prevent progressive corneal disease that may lead to irreversible blindness. The hospital’s rare-disease philanthropic fund has a single $2 million allotment that must be used now for one purpose: either to pay for this infant’s one-time experimental gene therapy, which has shown meaningful visual improvement in 30–40% of cases but carries a 5% risk of catastrophic immune-mediated organ failure and uncertain long-term results, or to fund a year-long statewide outreach, diagnostic testing, and care-navigation program projected to identify and connect 40–60 underserved, underdiagnosed infants to early interventions and specialty care. The parents urgently request the gene therapy for their child, stating no other funding is available. The outreach program is expected to halve time-to-diagnosis in marginalized regions and enable timely interventions for dozens of infants, but would use the entire fund, making the gene therapy unavailable for the newborn. The pediatric rare-disease allocation committee must decide on the single use of the fund with no alternative funding expected. What should the pediatric rare-disease allocation committee do?
Choice A: Approve funding for the newborn’s one-time experimental gene therapy now.
Choice B: Decline funding for the newborn’s therapy and allocate the funds to the year-long statewide outreach, diagnostic testing, and care-navigation program.

A 9-month-old infant with confirmed MGAT2-CDG has severe hypotonia, feeding failure requiring gastrostomy, progressive microcephaly, recurrent infections, impaired platelet aggregation, and brain atrophy, and the disease has already caused repeated hospitalizations. The center has one remaining slot this month for a one-time investigational therapy that is so expensive and scarce that the hospital uses an established review policy designed to direct the treatment to the child expected to benefit most, and this infant is only modestly lower on that metric than another child waiting for the same treatment. The parents have carefully reviewed the evidence, spoken with outside specialists, and can accurately explain the therapy’s limits and uncertainties; they still want their child to receive the slot now because they believe even a small chance of slowing decline is worth taking. The treating metabolic physician knows the family is fully informed, but also knows that choosing this infant would mean bypassing the center’s allocation policy and giving the slot to a child who is not the top candidate by the hospital’s metric. What should the treating metabolic physician do?
Choice A: Give the available treatment slot to this infant now.
Choice B: Allocate the treatment slot according to the center’s prioritization policy.

At 20 weeks’ gestation, a 32-year-old pregnant woman—alert, oriented, and fully capable of decision-making—has prenatal testing showing her male fetus is hemizygous for a pathogenic LAMP2 variant; the couple previously lost a son at age 6 to rapidly progressive Danon disease characterized by early dilated cardiomyopathy, severe developmental impairment, gait problems, and cardiorespiratory arrest. Fetal imaging is currently unremarkable, but in this family the disease typically produces catastrophic cardiac and neurologic decline in early childhood. A single-center, early-phase in utero AAV-mediated gene transfer research protocol is scheduled at 22 weeks; it is biologically plausible but unproven, with extremely limited human data and unknown long-term effects, and the procedure carries significant immediate risks to fetus and mother (procedure-related fetal loss, preterm delivery, maternal hemorrhage/infection, and potential impacts on future fertility). The alternative is to advise against prenatal intervention and plan intensive postnatal surveillance with expedited enrollment in postnatal trials and early transplant pathways when eligible—an established clinical pathway that may nevertheless only be available after irreversible organ injury in this family. The maternal-fetal medicine attending and multidisciplinary obstetric/research team, with input from the parents and institutional oversight, must decide whether to facilitate enrollment in the prenatal trial or to advise against it and pursue the postnatal pathway. What should the maternal-fetal medicine attending and multidisciplinary obstetric/research team do?
Choice A: Recommend and arrange enrollment in the available in utero AAV gene transfer research protocol at 22 weeks.
Choice B: Advise against the in utero procedure and instead plan for intensive postnatal surveillance with expedited postnatal treatment/transplant pathways.

Lucas is a 24-year-old man with genetically confirmed X-linked intellectual disability, Cabezas type (CUL4B), who has lifelong moderate intellectual disability, absent speech requiring assisted communication, progressive scoliosis, frequent aggressive outbursts, marked functional dependence, macrocephaly, and short stature; his symptoms began in early childhood and he is alert, oriented, and able to express stable preferences through his assistive device. A hospital-offered, one-time personalized gene-replacement therapy—restricted by the donor to a single patient, costing $2.5M in subsidy and requiring a dedicated ICU bed and two weeks of intensive, specialized navigation support—can be scheduled within a narrowly defined biologic window that the clinical team judges will close in about 6–8 weeks; if the therapy is not administered in that interval, the team considers the chance for meaningful improvement to be very unlikely. The hospital currently has the single donor-funded slot, the only appropriately equipped ICU bed available during that window, and the only two trained navigators who can coordinate the complex logistics; allocating those resources to Lucas would preclude using them simultaneously for outreach. Six under-served rare-disease families with comparable clinical need are on a validated waiting list but lack language access, stable insurance, and the advocacy to complete enrollment without immediate, dedicated outreach and navigation; with immediate institutional outreach using the donor funds and staff, clinicians estimate 2–3 of those families could realistically be brought to readiness within the coming months and receive the same therapy. The allocation committee must decide whether to schedule Lucas now with the donor-funded slot and the navigation team or to reserve the funds and staff for immediate targeted outreach to the under-served families—What should the allocation committee do?
Choice A: Use the donor-funded slot, the ICU bed, and the specialized navigation staff to treat Lucas now.
Choice B: Reserve the donor funds and navigation staff for immediate targeted outreach to the under-served rare-disease families on the waiting list.

disease: Palatal anomalies-widely spaced teeth-facial dysmorphism-developmental delay syndrome
vignette:
A 6-month-old infant with a confirmed pathogenic KDM1A variant presents with global developmental delay, severe hypotonia with recurrent aspiration requiring gastrostomy feeding, cleft palate, bilateral ptosis, and colpocephaly. The child is too young to make medical decisions. An experimental gene-replacement therapy is available under compassionate use, but published experience is limited, long-term outcomes are unknown, and the treatment carries a substantial risk of severe immune reaction, permanent morbidity, or death. Providing the therapy at this hospital would require reallocating approximately $2.5 million from the institution’s constrained rare-disease charity/innovation fund and would use the program’s only remaining compassionate-use/trial slot for the next 12–24 months, likely excluding several other children whom clinicians judge to be at imminent risk of death or irreversible decline without near-term access to funds or trial slots. The infant’s parents urgently request the therapy and the treating geneticist supports offering it; the pediatric resource-allocation committee must now decide whether to approve institutional funding and the single slot or to deny the request and continue medically appropriate supportive care while preserving funds and access for other patients. What should the pediatric hospital resource-allocation committee do?
Choice A: Approve and fund the compassionate-use gene therapy for this infant now.
Choice B: Deny the therapy; continue standard supportive care and preserve the fund and the program’s remaining compassionate-use/trial slot for other patients.

Miguel is a 10-year-old boy with genetically confirmed X-linked Emery–Dreifuss muscular dystrophy (pathogenic FHL1 variant); he is alert, oriented, and the treating team’s multidisciplinary capacity evaluation (genetics, pediatric neurology, pediatric cardiology, child psychology, and an independent assessor) found him able to understand and deliberately weigh complex medical choices. He has progressive proximal upper-limb weakness, elbow and Achilles contractures, early scoliosis, and conduction disease with frequent ventricular ectopy consistent with likely ongoing cardiac and neuromuscular decline beginning in childhood. A novel in vivo gene-editing infusion is available at the center under a compassionate protocol and could plausibly halt or reverse disease, but evidence is extremely limited, long-term effects are unpredictable, and there is a substantial immediate risk of severe inflammatory/toxic reaction and an estimated (but uncertain) ~8% risk of treatment-related fatal arrhythmia. Miguel’s preference to accept substantial risk after repeated counseling is stable and supported by his parents, yet the treating team feels conflicted between honoring his request and avoiding direct exposure of him to a high chance of serious harm; the alternative recommended pathway is ICD implantation plus optimized supportive care, which reduces near-term sudden-death risk but will not alter progressive muscle degeneration. What should the treating pediatric neuromuscular/genetics team do?
Choice A: Proceed now with the experimental in vivo gene-editing infusion under the compassionate protocol.
Choice B: Decline the infusion and proceed with ICD implantation and optimized supportive supportive care.

A 44-year-old man with genetically confirmed spinocerebellar ataxia type 40 due to a CCDC88C pathogenic variant has progressive dysarthria, scanning speech, dysmetria, broad-based gait, and vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, but he is alert, oriented, and fully capable of making decisions. His neurology team can offer only one funded slot this quarter for a one-time, extremely expensive investigational therapy that is being used under a limited access program, and there is no reliable evidence that a patient with his exact disease will benefit more than other rare ataxia patients. The only other eligible candidate is a woman with the same disorder who lives in a remote area, was diagnosed years later after repeated misdiagnoses, has never had access to a specialty ataxia clinic, and is now too disabled to travel easily for evaluation, making this likely her only realistic chance to receive the therapy. The treating neurologist and the hospital allocation committee must decide whether to use the single slot for the patient already under specialty care or to reserve it for the patient with greater barriers to reaching rare-disease treatment opportunities. What should the treating neurologist and hospital allocation committee do?
Choice A: Use the slot for the patient already under specialty care now
Choice B: Reserve the slot for the patient with greater access barriers

A metabolic geneticist is caring for a 10-month-old infant with confirmed MEND syndrome due to a pathogenic EBP variant, presenting with generalized hypotonia, cataracts, feeding difficulty, and developmental delay; the infant is alert, medically stable, and the parents understand that the proposed genome-directed treatment is experimental and not guaranteed to help. The hospital has one charity-funded slot this quarter for this intervention, and the program’s rules use a ranked waiting list to treat similarly affected rare-disease patients the same way. After learning that their child would likely lose the chance to receive the treatment if the team follows the queue, the parents ask the physician to bypass the list because they have already arranged travel, lost work, and a temporary relocation to take advantage of this one opening, and they state that delaying would amount to denying their child the only realistic chance they see. The physician knows that granting this request would likely push back another child with an equally severe rare disorder who has waited longer under the same rules, but refusing would mean this infant may not access the only available slot before the window closes. What should the treating metabolic geneticist and the hospital rare-disease allocation committee do?
Choice A: Use the charity-funded slot for this infant now.
Choice B: Reserve the slot for the next eligible patient under the allocation rules.

A 34-year-old woman with a confirmed pathogenic YY1 variant has recurrent fasting hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia from an insulinoma, with repeated episodes of confusion, tremor, and one seizure despite continuous dextrose, frequent feeds, and maximal medical therapy. Imaging suggests a small pancreatic lesion, but the endocrine surgeon says that removing it would likely require an operation with a substantial chance of major pancreatic injury, permanent brittle diabetes, or a prolonged ICU course, and there is no guarantee the hypoglycemia would be fully cured. The patient is alert, oriented, and fully capable of deciding, but she insists on surgery because she fears another hypoglycemic coma, while the team is uneasy about exposing her to a procedure that could leave her worse off than the disease. The treating physician, together with the endocrine surgery team, must decide whether to proceed with high-risk surgery now or continue intensive nonoperative management and surveillance. What should the treating physician with the endocrine surgery team do?
Choice A: Proceed with high-risk surgery now
Choice B: Defer surgery and continue intensive medical management and surveillance

A newborn boy with confirmed 20p12.3 microdeletion syndrome has macrocephaly, midface hypoplasia, global developmental delay, and Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome; despite maximal ward support, he is now having recurrent unstable tachyarrhythmias and intermittent respiratory failure. The tertiary children’s hospital has one open ICU bed, and the transfer center has two urgent requests: this infant for continuous monitoring and possible electrophysiology intervention, and another infant who is also critically ill but has a more predictable response to ICU care and a shorter expected stay. The electrophysiology team says this newborn’s course is uncertain but still plausibly reversible if he reaches the ICU now, while delaying transfer could mean he deteriorates beyond rescue; however, accepting him would almost certainly block the other infant from the only bed and may leave several hours of transport, staffing, and specialist time unavailable for a patient with a clearer chance of benefit. The treating team cannot admit both, and the family is asking for “whatever gives him the best chance,” while the hospital is also under pressure to use the last ICU bed where it is most likely to help the greatest number of children. What should the treating ICU and transfer team do?
Choice A: Reserve the ICU bed for the newborn and transfer him for specialized care now.
Choice B: Allocate the ICU bed to the other infant and keep the newborn on lower-intensity support while awaiting capacity.

disease: Cognitive impairment-coarse facies-heart defects-obesity-pulmonary involvement-short stature-skeletal dysplasia syndrome
vignette:
At 24 weeks’ gestation, a pregnant woman is carrying a fetus with a confirmed pathogenic AFF4 variant and ultrasound findings already showing severe skeletal abnormalities, microcephaly, a cardiac defect, and early pulmonary involvement, and the team has explained that the child is likely to need prolonged intensive care with uncertain long-term function even if born alive. A fetal therapy center offers a one-time in-utero gene-editing procedure only through a tightly restricted compassionate-use protocol, with no comparable option available elsewhere, and the mother repeatedly shows that she understands the limits of the evidence, can explain the potential benefits and risks in her own words, and remains consistent in asking to proceed because she would accept the chance of fetal loss or major injury for any possibility of changing the child’s course. The treating maternal-fetal medicine physician knows that the protocol allows enrollment only if the center’s ethics committee agrees that the anticipated harm is not disproportionate, yet also knows that refusing the request will leave the family with no other disease-modifying option and may condemn the fetus to a course the mother believes would be intolerable. The physician must decide whether to enroll the pregnancy and perform the procedure or decline and continue only supportive prenatal care. What should the treating maternal-fetal medicine physician do?
Choice A: Enroll the pregnancy and proceed with the in-utero gene-editing procedure.
Choice B: Decline the procedure and continue supportive prenatal care only.

A 2-day-old newborn with confirmed pathogenic RBM10 variants and prenatal findings consistent with TARP syndrome—including severe micrognathia, Pierre-Robin sequence, glossoptosis, persistent left superior vena cava, cerebellar hypoplasia, generalized hypotonia, cyanotic spells, and failure to thrive—remains alert but has repeated oxygen desaturations during handling and feeds. The NICU and ENT teams agree the airway is unstable, but not in immediate collapse; they estimate that the baby may remain supportable for another 12–18 hours with careful positioning and noninvasive oxygen, though any worsening could turn a controlled procedure into an emergency. The parents understand the diagnosis and the likely need for a tracheostomy, but they have spent the last day trying to reconcile conflicting expert opinions about whether to proceed with a procedure that would likely mean prolonged intensive care, repeated interventions, and significant suffering in a condition with very limited evidence. The treating neonatologist must decide whether to move forward with tracheostomy before the parents finish deliberating, or continue temporizing support long enough for them to make a settled decision. What should the treating neonatologist do?
Choice A: Proceed with tracheostomy now
Choice B: Continue temporizing support and allow additional time for family deliberation

A 28-year-old patient with biallelic DSG4 pathogenic variants causing lifelong near-total scalp and body hair loss (onset age 1–10 years) reports months of disabling social withdrawal and deteriorating mental health despite counseling and prosthetic options. A biotech company offers a personalized ex vivo gene-editing keratinocyte transplant that produced durable hair regrowth in two compassionate-use cases but remains investigational; it carries a small, plausible risk of clonal expansion and treatment-related malignancy and has uncertain long-term safety and generalizability. The treatment price is $2.1 million and the hospital’s rare-disease philanthropy fund contains exactly that amount; the fund is explicitly earmarked to support basic, urgent services for multiple rare-disease patients, and spending it now would exhaust the fund and prevent support planned this year for three children’s ongoing enzyme-replacement programs and one patient’s bridge to a lifesaving transplant. The patient is alert, oriented, demonstrates clear factual understanding of the therapy’s likely benefits, uncertainties, and risks, and requests that the hospital use the fund to pay for the treatment. What should the hospital rare-disease philanthropy allocation committee do?
Choice A: Approve use of the hospital’s rare-disease philanthropy fund to pay for the patient’s personalized gene-editing keratinocyte therapy.
Choice B: Decline to use the hospital’s fund for this treatment, preserve the fund for planned basic, urgent services for multiple patients, and offer the patient maximal unfunded supportive care plus prioritized placement on research and clinical-trial waitlists.

A 7-year-old boy with genetically confirmed progressive myoclonic epilepsy type 3 due to biallelic KCTD7 variants has myoclonus, focal seizures with secondary generalization, progressive truncal ataxia, developmental regression, and cerebral atrophy despite multiple antiseizure medications. He is alert, oriented, and able to explain in his own words why he wants to try a first-in-human gene therapy that is available only through a single-slot trial: he says he understands that it might help slow his decline, but also might not help at all and could still cause serious brain inflammation or prolonged hospitalization. Over three separate conversations with the neurology, genetics, and research teams, he gives the same reasoned answer, can compare the options, and does not change his mind when his parents leave the room; his parents disagree with each other and ask the clinicians to decide whether his request is mature enough to honor. The trial has no alternative candidate for this opening, and declining now would close the only chance to enroll before further neurologic loss, but proceeding would expose him to a treatment with uncertain benefit and meaningful risk of severe, possibly irreversible harm. What should the treating pediatric neurologist, with the genetics and research teams, do?
Choice A: Support enrollment in the investigational gene therapy trial
Choice B: Decline enrollment and continue optimized supportive care

A metabolic geneticist is caring for a 6-week-old girl with MECP2-related severe neonatal encephalopathy, who has generalized neonatal hypotonia, multifocal epileptiform discharges, recurrent seizures, gastrostomy tube feeding, microcephaly, and worsening respiratory insufficiency. The team believes she could be transferred to the pediatric ICU for a one-time investigational infusion before her next decline but not after. The hospital has only one ICU slot and one charity-funded infusion available this month, and two infants with the same rare disease meet the eligibility criteria within days of each other. One infant is this girl, whose family lives nearby and reached the specialty center quickly; the other infant has had repeated missed diagnoses, months of travel barriers, and delayed referral, and is now also at high risk of near-term respiratory failure if treatment is delayed again. The allocation committee cannot separate them on clinical grounds alone because both are seriously ill and both may worsen without prompt treatment, but choosing the local family now would leave the longer-waiting child without the only realistic chance to receive care this month. What should the allocation committee do?
Choice A: Use the ICU slot and charity-funded infusion for this infant now.
Choice B: Defer this infant and allocate the ICU slot and charity-funded infusion to the longer-waiting infant.

A 30-year-old woman, who is alert, oriented, and fully capable of decision-making, is 18 weeks pregnant and prenatal testing indicates the fetus almost certainly carries a pathogenic RUNX2 variant causing cleidocranial dysplasia with severe, early-onset skeletal, dental, hearing, and respiratory problems. Her older child has the same diagnosis, requires lifelong, publicly funded surgical and hearing care, and the family already receives multiple state-supported services; preventing the predictable suffering of another affected child is central to the mother’s reproductive and parental decisions. A state-funded perinatal gene therapy program has a single slot this year; limited neonatal reports show marked short-term anatomical improvements in a few treated infants but long-term durability is unknown and rare serious harms have been reported in isolated cases, and the slot’s cost equals funding dozens of other pediatric interventions or several population-level programs. The pregnant woman formally requests that the allocation committee reserve the single available slot for her fetus; the committee must now decide whether to approve or deny that request. What should the state Medicaid allocation committee do?
Choice A: Approve the allocation and reserve the single perinatal RUNX2 gene therapy slot for this fetus.
Choice B: Deny the allocation and reallocate the funds/slot toward programs intended to maximize overall pediatric health benefit.

A 10-month-old infant with genetically confirmed biallelic RPGRIP1L variants presents with severe neurologic symptoms and rapidly progressive liver disease. The parents, acting as legal surrogates, request all possible interventions and have identified an experimental gene therapy that, if combined with a pediatric liver transplant, could potentially improve the infant's condition but carries significant perioperative risk and uncertain long-term outcomes. Proceeding would require allocating a marginal pediatric donor liver and an institutional subsidy of about $2.5 million, resources that could otherwise support several other children on the transplant waitlist who have higher projected long-term survival with standard transplant and could also benefit broader program support for indigent pediatric patients. The pediatric transplant committee must decide whether to approve listing and commit the organ and subsidy for this infant or to decline and prioritize other candidates, knowing that either choice will have serious consequences. What should the pediatric transplant committee do?
Choice A: Approve listing, commit the donor liver and institutional subsidy, and pursue the combined gene therapy plus transplant for this infant.
Choice B: Decline to allocate the donor liver and subsidy for this case, prioritize other transplant candidates per standard allocation, and provide best available supportive/palliative care for the infant.

A 42-year-old person with genetically confirmed Tangier disease is experiencing severe coronary and carotid artery stenosis, left ventricular hypertrophy, recurrent abdominal pain from hepatosplenomegaly, distal muscle weakness with peripheral axonal neuropathy, facial diplegia, thrombocytopenia, nail dystrophy, and worsening functional decline despite optimal supportive care. A personalized, one-time gene therapy was recently authorized under an accelerated pathway based on limited data showing halted biochemical progression in about 65% of treated patients at 18 months and partial neurologic improvement in about 20%; durability beyond three years is uncertain and the therapy carries a 1.5% risk of catastrophic complications such as organ failure or death. The therapy costs $2.5 million, and current manufacturing limits mean the hospital has a single dose available this year for an identified patient; hospital modeling estimates that using this dose for the present patient would produce an estimated 35 quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs) for that individual. Alternatively, reallocating the $2.5 million would create a five-year regional program of expanded newborn and family screening, long-term subsidized specialty care, and targeted interventions projected to identify and benefit about 40 patients and yield an estimated 150 QALYs across the region; the modeling includes uncertainty ranges but favors greater aggregate population benefit from the program. The hospital’s rare-disease allocation committee must choose whether to allocate the single dose to this identified patient now or to redirect the funds to the regional program that would likely produce greater total benefit across many affected people. What should the hospital’s rare-disease allocation committee do?
Choice A: Allocate the single available one-time gene therapy dose to this patient now.
Choice B: Deny allocation to this patient and redirect the $2.5M to the regional screening and subsidy program.

A 5-month-old girl with biallelic pathogenic variants in PRUNE1 has had symptoms since birth, including severe axial hypotonia, epileptic spasms, delayed myelination, early cerebral and cerebellar atrophy, reflux with poor feeding, and worsening respiratory insufficiency now requiring nighttime noninvasive ventilation. She is receiving optimized seizure, nutrition, respiratory, rehabilitation, and palliative-supportive care, and there is no approved disease-modifying treatment for PRUNE1-related neurological syndrome. A research hospital has emergency access to a personalized intrathecal gene-correction product for her exact variant; animal and organoid studies show biologic correction when given early, but the same delivery approach in closely related ultra-rare neurologic disorders has caused severe inflammatory injury in a small minority of treated children, including death and irreversible paralysis. The treating specialists agree that immediate treatment and deferral are both medically defensible: treating now may be the only remaining chance to slow further brain loss before continuous ventilatory dependence or fixed severe spastic tetraparesis closes eligibility, while waiting 3–6 months may reduce uncertainty but will likely allow additional irreversible neurologic and respiratory decline. Her parents request treatment, but the hospital advanced-therapeutics committee must decide whether the possibility of preserving remaining function justifies exposing a medically fragile infant to a poorly quantified risk of catastrophic treatment-related suffering, disability, or death. What should the hospital advanced-therapeutics committee do?
Choice A: Authorize immediate intrathecal personalized PRUNE1 gene-correction therapy.
Choice B: Defer gene-correction therapy and continue optimized supportive care while awaiting additional safety data.

A 28-year-old woman, alert and oriented and repeatedly counseled by genetics and maternal–fetal medicine teams, is 22 weeks pregnant and prenatal testing indicates the fetus almost certainly carries a pathogenic GDF5 variant consistent with fibular aplasia–complex brachydactyly syndrome with severe limb malformations and predicted lifelong major mobility limitations. The hospital controls the region’s only in-utero, one-time gene therapy slot that could plausibly alter skeletal development but carries substantial uncertainty about effectiveness, nontrivial risks including fetal loss and severe inflammatory complications, and a multi-million-dollar per-patient cost constrained by manufacturing and regulatory capacity. The woman demonstrates clear understanding of the procedure’s uncertain harms and benefits, has deliberated with the care team and an independent ethics consultant across multiple visits, and persistently requests that this fetus receive this year’s single slot. The hospital allocation committee’s probabilistic prioritization model projects that allocating the slot to alternative candidate(s) (for example, treating two or more postnatal children with other rare disorders) would likely yield a higher expected cumulative population-level benefit under current assumptions, but those projections have wide confidence intervals and are contested by some clinicians; the committee must decide whether to honor the mother’s considered request or reserve the slot to maximize expected benefit across patients. What should the hospital allocation committee do?
Choice A: Approve enrollment of this fetus in the hospital’s single in‑utero gene therapy slot.
Choice B: Deny enrollment and reserve the therapy slot to allocate according to a policy that prioritizes maximizing overall population benefit.

disease: Severe neonatal hypotonia-seizures-encephalopathy syndrome due to 5q31.3 microdeletion
vignette:
An 8-month-old infant with a confirmed 5q31.3 microdeletion affecting PURA presents with progressive refractory seizures, severe feeding impairment with recurrent aspiration, early brain atrophy with delayed myelination, and chronic respiratory compromise; without intervention, the likely trajectory is severe, lifelong neurological disability but not imminently terminal. The infant is legally incapable of decision-making; the parents, after multiple multidisciplinary counseling sessions and review of the limited preclinical evidence and nontrivial risk of catastrophic adverse effects, request that the hospital manufacture and administer a first-in-human individualized viral gene-replacement under compassionate access. The hospital’s GMP gene-therapy facility can produce only one individualized dose per quarter, and allocating that slot and an estimated $1.5–2.0M subsidy to this infant would delay a randomized early-phase trial by an estimated 6–12 months, prevent timely treatment for several children currently on the trial waitlist, and risk slowing or jeopardizing regulatory and funding milestones that could expand access to many patients. The multi-disciplinary allocation committee recognizes that both approving and declining are clinically defensible but entail substantial consequences for the family and for many other children; they must decide how to proceed. What should the hospital’s gene-therapy access and resource-allocation committee do?
Choice A: Approve manufacture and administration of an individualized viral gene-replacement product for this infant now, funded by the hospital/philanthropic subsidy.
Choice B: Decline the one-off manufacture request to preserve the manufacturing slot and funds for the randomized trial and other patients; continue optimized supportive care, registry enrollment, and palliative planning for the infant.

disease: Non-acquired combined pituitary hormone deficiency-sensorineural hearing loss-spine abnormalities syndrome
vignette:
A newborn with a confirmed homozygous pathogenic LHX3 variant presents with combined pituitary hormone deficiency, sensorineural hearing loss, spine abnormalities, anterior pituitary hypoplasia, ACTH deficiency, central hypothyroidism, short stature, and bilateral sensorineural hearing impairment evident at birth. The infant is stabilized on lifelong hormone replacement and hearing support, which permit survival but will not reverse multisystem deficits. The parents, both known carriers who previously lost an affected child to the same condition, are the infant’s surrogates and request immediate enrollment in a one-time compassionate-use gene-replacement trial offered at this center, expressing a strong family imperative to pursue a potential corrective intervention. Preliminary reports from the developer estimate a 25–40% chance of meaningful endocrine improvement, a 10–15% risk of severe immune-mediated complications including death or permanent neurologic injury, and no reliable long-term outcome data, leaving substantial uncertainty about net lifelong benefit. The therapy would require approximately $2.0 million from the hospital’s constrained rare-disease fund and would occupy the program’s sole experimental trial slot for 18–24 months, likely delaying or preventing access for several other children on the waiting list with progressive, time-sensitive conditions who would otherwise be candidates for interventions expected to provide measurable benefits across the broader patient population. The hospital rare-disease allocation committee must decide whether to approve enrollment and commit the fund and slot to this infant or to decline and preserve the resources for broader allocation while continuing standard lifelong hormone replacement and supportive care. What should the hospital rare-disease allocation committee do?
Choice A: Approve compassionate-use enrollment and allocate the ~$2.0M fund and the single trial slot to this infant.
Choice B: Decline enrollment for this infant, preserve the fund and trial slot for broader allocation, and continue standard lifelong hormone replacement and supportive care.

A 9-month-old infant with genetically confirmed biallelic pathogenic MMP14 variants (Multicentric osteolysis-nodulosis-arthropathy spectrum) has rapidly progressive osteolysis of the upper and lower limbs, abnormal hand morphology, painful joint contractures, failure to sit, and escalating opioid-dependent pain despite comprehensive supportive care. The parents, after multiple clinic discussions, documented questions, and consultations with the specialty center and patient networks, have carefully deliberated and request transfer to a distant center offering an ex vivo gene-correction protocol that requires myeloablative conditioning; published experience is extremely limited and outcomes are uncertain. The specialty center will only accept the infant if the local treating pediatric geneticist formally endorses and arranges transfer; without that endorsement transfer is effectively blocked. The experimental pathway carries substantial risks (treatment-related mortality, multi-organ toxicity, prolonged immunosuppression, and unknown late effects), and the local transplant service and hospital ethics committee are divided or unavailable to provide a timely recommendation, leaving the geneticist as the decisive gatekeeper between the parents’ request and continued conservative care; the family says denial would be devastating while the clinician worries endorsement could expose the infant to immediate, serious harms. What should the treating pediatric geneticist do?
Choice A: Endorse and arrange transfer for the infant to receive the ex vivo gene-correction protocol (proceed with the experimental therapy pathway).
Choice B: Decline to endorse transfer and continue conservative supportive care locally (decline experimental therapy and prioritize avoiding treatment-related harms).

A 16-year-old girl with genetically confirmed Mulibrey nanism is being considered for a one-time investigational treatment offered through a single regional rare-disease slot. The therapy is highly resource-intensive, with no strong comparative data and no guarantee of meaningful benefit, and the hospital has agreed to fund only one case this quarter. Another eligible patient on the waitlist has already demonstrated a clear understanding of the uncertainties involved. During counseling, the patient expresses her desire for the treatment based on her mother's assurance that it will "almost certainly fix" her disease, but she herself cannot accurately explain the likely limits or the possibility that the therapy may not help at all. The treating geneticist and allocation committee must decide whether to submit her application now or delay it until she demonstrates a realistic understanding of what is known and unknown, knowing that delay may mean losing the only available slot to a different patient who can make a more informed decision about the same scarce resource. What should the treating geneticist and allocation committee do?
Choice A: Submit the application and move forward with treatment now
Choice B: Delay the application until she demonstrates a realistic understanding of the treatment’s uncertainties and limits

A transplant committee is reviewing the case of a 4-month-old boy with confirmed GATA6-related pancreatic hypoplasia-diabetes-congenital heart disease syndrome, who has pancreatic aplasia, feeding difficulties, intermittent diarrhea, neonatal hypotonia, a ventricular septal defect, and prolonged dependence on intensive care support. His parents are alert, consistently engaged, and able to explain the diagnosis and the team’s recommendation, but they have also read several recent case reports and insist on using the center’s last available pediatric high-acuity slot for a combined procedure that could be attempted now rather than waiting for the usual pathway. The committee knows that approving this request would consume a highly limited resource that could otherwise go to other children on the waiting list whose cases more cleanly meet the center’s allocation rules and who may otherwise lose their only realistic chance at treatment this season. The treating physician must decide whether to honor the parents’ informed request to pursue the expedited pathway or defer it in order to preserve the scarce opportunity for the broader waiting list. What should the treating physician do?
Choice A: Honor the parents’ request and pursue the expedited pathway now.
Choice B: Defer the request and reserve the scarce opportunity for the broader waiting list.

A 46-year-old man with genetically confirmed AGel amyloidosis (GSN) has progressive sensory neuropathy, bilateral ptosis, keratoconjunctivitis sicca, bruising susceptibility, proteinuria, and worsening daily function despite standard supportive care, and his rare-disease team is considering the center’s last available dose of a very expensive infusion that is stocked through a fixed charity program. The same dose could instead be assigned to a different patient on the program’s waitlist with another ultra-rare disorder; both patients are stable enough to wait a short time, both are reasonable candidates, and the expected benefit for each is uncertain and roughly comparable. The allocation committee knows that giving the dose to this man would honor equal access across rare diseases that already consume extraordinary resources, but it would also mean forgoing a chance to direct the only remaining dose toward the patient the committee believes is more likely to produce the greatest total health gain for the program’s limited supply. The committee must decide whether to use the final dose for him now or reserve it for the other waitlisted patient. What should the allocation committee do?
Choice A: Give the final dose to this patient now.
Choice B: Reserve the final dose for the other waitlisted patient expected to produce greater total benefit.

A 2-day-old girl with biallelic ALOX12B variants has self-improving collodion baby complicated by marked skin tightness, painful fissuring, and limited hand and ankle movement, and the team expects weeks of intensive skin care before she can safely leave the NICU. A hospital-run neonatal skin-protection program could reduce scarring risk, but it requires a specialized NICU bed, daily input from a burn-surgery team, and a compounded emollient that the hospital can obtain for only one infant this month under a temporary access agreement. A second newborn with a different rare genetic skin disorder has been waiting longer for the same program and lives several hours away from any center that can provide it, while this baby’s family already receives care at the tertiary hospital and could return reliably for close follow-up if the slot is deferred. The treating neonatologist and the hospital allocation committee must decide whether to use the only available program slot now for this infant or reserve it for the other newborn whose access to comparable care is much more limited. What should the treating neonatologist and the hospital allocation committee do?
Choice A: Use the only available program slot for the ALOX12B-affected newborn now.
Choice B: Reserve the program slot for the other newborn with much more limited access.

disease: X-linked intellectual disability due to GRIA3 mutations
vignette:
A rare-disease geneticist is caring for a 16-year-old boy with confirmed GRIA3-related intellectual disability, global developmental delay, axial hypotonia, seizures, gait instability, and autistic behaviors; he is alert, oriented, and judged fully capable of understanding his situation and expressing a stable choice. He has been offered enrollment in a one-time expanded-access protocol for an investigational gene-based therapy, but the treatment requires a fixed infusion date this month and the program has made clear that if he declines now, the slot cannot be held and will be reassigned to another child with a different rare disorder who is already losing eligibility because of age and disease progression. The team believes the therapy is worth considering but cannot predict whether it will help, and the infusion itself carries meaningful risk of prolonged hospitalization and possible neurologic worsening. The patient says he understands the tradeoffs but does not want to proceed because he does not want to accept the chance of a major setback for a benefit he sees as too uncertain, while his parents ask the team to override him so the scarce slot is not "wasted" when another child could receive it. What should the treating geneticist and rare-disease program team do?
Choice A: Proceed with the treatment despite the patient’s refusal.
Choice B: Respect the patient’s refusal and release the slot to another eligible child.

A 9-year-old boy with pathogenic biallelic TDO2 variants has progressive hypertryptophanemia with increased serum serotonin, severe headaches, poor sleep, and declining school function; a newly available custom enzyme-modulating therapy might slow the disease, but the evidence is thin, the monitoring burden is intense, and the program costs over $1 million per year. He is alert, oriented, and can clearly explain why he wants to start, but when the team asks him to compare the uncertain personal benefit against the chance that another equally eligible child could lose the last subsidized program slot, he repeats a highly fixed explanation that the treatment feels “meant for me” and dismisses the broader impact despite repeated discussion. The hospital’s rare-disease subsidy has only one remaining enrollment slot this year, and using it for this child would almost certainly exclude another child with the same diagnosis who meets the same eligibility criteria but has no alternate funding. The treating metabolic physician must decide whether to submit this boy for the final slot or follow the center’s standard first-come, first-served policy. What should the treating metabolic physician do?
Choice A: Submit the boy for the final subsidized treatment slot.
Choice B: Follow the standard allocation policy and keep the final slot available for another equally eligible patient.

A 19-year-old man with genetically confirmed Rothmund–Thomson syndrome type 1 (ANAPC1) has lifelong severe manifestations including transfusion-dependent myelodysplasia, recurrent pathologic fractures, progressive cutaneous malignancies, profound short stature, and chronic immune dysfunction; he is alert, oriented, and fully capable of making medical decisions. A novel ex vivo gene-replacement therapy, available through a single publicly subsidized manufacturing slot this year, has produced durable remissions in a very small trial but carries a nontrivial risk of fatal conditioning toxicity and uncertain long-term durability; administration requires intensive inpatient resources and approximately $2.5M in public funds. The hospital allocates this single annual slot by a blind lottery among five currently eligible patients to give each similarly eligible candidate an equal chance; the four other eligible patients include a 6-year-old with transfusion-dependent marrow failure, a newborn with rapidly progressive growth and feeding failure, a 45-year-old with recurrent skin cancers and limited social support, and a 16-year-old with severe immune dysfunction and frequent hospitalizations. Treating teams report no clear way to rank the five candidates by likely benefit, and the patient, after detailed counseling about risks, benefits, and uncertainties, requests that the hospital approve use of the slot and funds for him now. The hospital allocation committee must decide whether to approve the slot and funding for this patient or to adhere to the established lottery process. What should the hospital allocation committee do?
Choice A: Approve and allocate the single manufacturing slot and public/subsidized funds to offer the gene-replacement therapy to this patient now.
Choice B: Deny allocation for this patient and follow the hospital’s equal-access lottery so the slot and funds are distributed according to the established process among eligible patients.

A 24-year-old woman with genetically confirmed Rothmund–Thomson syndrome type 2 has experienced infant-onset poikiloderma, recurrent keratinocyte skin cancers with multiple resections, progressive cytopenias now requiring intermittent transfusions, severe skeletal fragility with repeated fractures, and marked functional decline despite years of supportive care. An early-phase overseas ex vivo autologous hematopoietic stem-cell gene-editing trial offers a chance of durable correction but has only very limited follow-up, unknown long-term benefit, and requires myeloablative conditioning with an estimated 5–10% peri-procedural mortality risk and substantial risks of long-term treatment-related morbidity, including infertility and secondary malignancy. The trial will enroll only patients for whom the local treating hematologist provides a signed attestation of suitability and the institution’s transplant committee supports referral; without that local attestation, the patient is extremely unlikely to find another center willing to accept the clinical and regulatory risks. The patient is alert, oriented, demonstrates coherent understanding and stable, reasoned reasons for wanting to pursue the trial despite its risks, and asks her treating hematologist to provide the required written attestation. The hematologist is unsure whether to provide that attestation or to decline and continue with conservative/supportive care locally. What should the treating hematologist do?
Choice A: Provide the required written attestation and refer the patient for enrollment in the overseas gene-editing transplant trial.
Choice B: Decline to provide the attestation and continue with local conservative/supportive management without facilitating trial referral.

disease: X-linked intellectual disability-global development delay-facial dysmorphism-sacral caudal remnant syndrome
vignette:
A state-funded program has only one available in-utero gene therapy slot this quarter for severe prenatally-manifesting TAF1-related disease, a rare genetic condition with uncertain natural history and limited evidence about treatment benefit. Two competent pregnant patients each carry a fetus with the same pathogenic TAF1 variant and overlapping but not identical prenatal findings. Patient 1, at 18 weeks, has fetal MRI showing more marked corpus callosum hypoplasia and early ventriculomegaly, findings that many specialists consider suggestive of greater near-term risk, though their predictive value for long-term outcome is unreliable. Patient 2, at 20 weeks, has subtler prenatal imaging but lives in a rural county, lacks private insurance, has unreliable transportation, and no nearby multidisciplinary neonatal neurodevelopmental, feeding, or epilepsy services, making consistent postnatal follow-up and participation in required longitudinal monitoring highly unlikely without intensive, costly support. Experts agree there is genuine uncertainty about which fetus is likely to derive the greater durable benefit from the single available, extremely costly, and logistically demanding intervention, and the allocation committee must decide which fetus will receive the slot. What should the state rare-disease therapy allocation committee do?
Choice A: Allocate the single in-utero therapy slot to the fetus with more pronounced prenatal indicators (the 18-week pregnancy).
Choice B: Allocate the single in-utero therapy slot to the fetus from the rural, low-income 20-week pregnancy with substantial barriers to follow-up care.

A 20-year-old man with genetically confirmed X-linked Emery–Dreifuss muscular dystrophy has progressive muscle weakness, contractures, and early hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with intermittent arrhythmias; he is alert, oriented, and has repeatedly demonstrated clear, stable, well-reasoned decisions about his care. A one-time gene-replacement product produced in limited batches offers a plausible chance of meaningful motor and cardiac stabilization based on early data, though there is a risk of severe immune-mediated liver injury. The center has the last available vial of a currently distributed batch; the sponsor reports that enrolling one more eligible participant now would trigger a pre-specified interim analysis and likely accelerate regulatory review and scaled manufacturing, advancing broader access by an estimated 12–24 months, whereas diverting the vial for off-trial compassionate use would probably delay that milestone by approximately 6–9 months. The patient, after detailed discussion, requests immediate off-trial compassionate administration and demonstrates understanding of the risks and uncertainties; the treating physician also serves as a voting member of the institutional allocation/enrollment committee and must choose whether to authorize off-trial administration now or reserve the vial for trial enrollment. What should the treating physician do?
Choice A: Authorize off-trial (compassionate-use) administration of the last available vial to this patient now.
Choice B: Reserve the last available vial for the pivotal trial (or allocate it to a trial participant selected to maximize generalizability), denying immediate off-trial access to this patient.

A 30-year-old pregnant woman, who is alert and oriented, presents at 18 weeks after prenatal testing identified a pathogenic PRDM8 variant in her fetus. With a previously affected sibling and the variant’s known course, clinicians judge the fetus highly likely to develop early-onset progressive myoclonus epilepsy with rapid neurologic decline in childhood. A recently approved gene-replacement therapy, intended to be given shortly after birth, has extremely limited follow-up data: registry reports of 50 treated infants show roughly 30% meaningful stabilization, about 40% minimal change, and around 30% serious complications including prolonged ICU stays, so long-term benefit and risk remain uncertain. Providing this therapy for the newborn would require a one-time institutional subsidy of about $2 million, which would exhaust the hospital’s last available philanthropic grant and make the hospital unable to fund any other new initiatives this fiscal year; hospital finance and philanthropy leadership say no realistic alternative funding is likely within the required time window. That same earmarked grant was pledged to start a focused outreach-and-support program to improve diagnostic access and care linkage for underserved low-income and minority children with rare neurologic disorders, with pilot-based projections of identifying 40–60 undiagnosed children over two years and directly linking 25–35 to care coordination and basic therapies. Choosing one use of the grant will foreclose the other. What should the hospital pediatric rare-disease allocation committee do?
Choice A: Approve the $2 million subsidy to cover the newborn’s gene-replacement therapy after birth.
Choice B: Reserve the grant to launch the outreach-and-support program and offer the family standard supportive care without institutional subsidy for the gene therapy.

A 22-year-old woman with genetically confirmed metatropic dysplasia has severe short stature, progressive cervical deformity, a narrow chest with marked thoracic restriction, progressive scoliosis, and chronic hypoventilation requiring nightly noninvasive ventilation. She is alert, oriented, and repeatedly demonstrates capacity to understand and reason about complex medical information. An overseas early-phase systemic AAV gene therapy program reports rare case series of substantial functional gains in a few young patients but also documents several cases of fulminant hyperinflammatory reactions causing rapid respiratory collapse and death. Her multidisciplinary team judges that, given her specific anatomy and ventilatory fragility, catastrophic peri-treatment respiratory failure is highly likely despite aggressive risk-reduction planning. After multiple detailed counseling sessions and time to reflect, she consistently and coherently requests that her treating physician actively endorse and coordinate referral, transfer logistics, and peri-treatment planning to pursue enrollment. The treating physician and team are deeply divided: some clinicians view active coordination and a written referral as appropriate support for a competent patient’s deliberated choice, while others view active facilitation as participating in an intervention likely to cause catastrophic harm. The physician must decide whether to actively support coordination or to refuse active facilitation and continue optimized supportive care, monitoring, and advance care planning. What should the treating physician do?
Choice A: Actively endorse and coordinate referral, transfer logistics, and peri-treatment planning with the overseas early-phase systemic AAV program to pursue enrollment.
Choice B: Decline to provide active endorsement or coordination for the experimental therapy given judged high peri-treatment risk, and continue optimized supportive care, monitoring, and advance care planning (while providing neutral informational resources if requested).

disease: Infantile-onset generalized dyskinesia with orofacial involvement
vignette:
A 28-year-old competent pregnant woman at 20 weeks’ gestation has CVS-confirmed biallelic pathogenic PDE10A variants identical to her older child, who developed severe infantile-onset generalized dyskinesia with prominent chorea, orofacial dyskinesia, dysarthria, feeding failure, and progressive motor decline beginning in infancy. Targeted fetal ultrasound shows intermittent exaggerated orofacial jerks but otherwise appropriate growth; after independent research, multiple counseling sessions, and documented deliberation, she requests enrollment in the center’s experimental in-utero AAV gene therapy under the hospital’s compassionate-access pathway, citing preliminary animal studies and a handful of neonatal reports that suggest prenatal delivery could plausibly prevent or markedly reduce the syndrome’s irreversible progression if given before birth. The maternal–fetal surgical team recognizes the procedure carries measurable risks—including fetal loss, potential off-target developmental effects, and significant maternal morbidity (hemorrhage, infection, anesthetic complications)—and notes the institutional review board has declined approval of a formal prenatal trial because of maternal risk, leaving compassionate-access approval to the treating team under restrictive institutional policy; deferring therapy until after birth avoids prenatal procedural harms but would very likely allow early, irreversible neurodevelopmental deterioration in the infant. What should the maternal–fetal surgical team do?
Choice A: Approve and offer the experimental in-utero AAV gene therapy under a tightly controlled compassionate-use protocol with enhanced maternal–fetal monitoring and documented informed consent.
Choice B: Decline prenatal intervention and recommend deferral to postnatal management and early supportive care, while prioritizing perinatal planning and enrollment in postnatal trials when available.

A 2-week-old infant with a pathogenic FGFR2 variant presents with early bilateral coronal craniosynostosis, feeding difficulties requiring nasogastric support, hand anomalies, and emerging signs of neurodevelopmental risk that are likely to lead to repeated high-risk craniofacial surgeries and significant long-term impairment if the current trajectory continues. The hospital has only one treatment slot this year for a novel in vivo FGFR2-targeted gene-editing therapy; early data suggest a 30–60% chance of altering the disease course, a substantial chance of no benefit, and a 5% risk of severe systemic inflammatory complication. Approving this infant would use the only slot and consume about 65% of the program’s rare-therapy funds for the year, which would reduce the program’s ability to treat several other children, including one with a rapidly progressive metabolic disorder and higher short-term mortality risk and another whose condition reliably responds to available therapy but is awaiting allocation. The infant’s parents urgently request access; the treating neonatologist and craniofacial team largely support offering the experimental option, while the allocation committee is divided and concerned about leaving other patients without timely care. The committee must now choose whether to approve the infant’s access to the gene-editing slot or preserve the slot and funds for other patients—What should the hospital’s rare-therapies allocation committee do?
Choice A: Approve and allocate the single available FGFR2 gene-editing treatment for this infant now.
Choice B: Decline allocation of the gene-editing treatment for this infant and continue with standard surgical and supportive care while preserving the slot and funds for other patients this year.

A 3-month-old infant with genetically confirmed ATAD1 hereditary hyperekplexia experiences frequent startle-induced apneas, marked myoclonus and hypertonia, failure to thrive requiring gastrostomy feeds, recurrent esophagitis, and early global developmental impairment; without intervention, clinicians estimate a high risk of profound lifelong disability and early mortality. A biotech compassionate-use program has offered a single in vivo gene-replacement therapy slot this year, requiring a $2.5M hospital/philanthropic commitment to cover treatment and peri-procedural care; evidence is limited to preclinical studies and very early human experience, showing large gains in some cases but also significant uncertainty about efficacy and risks, including possible serious adverse effects or treatment failure. Alternatively, the hospital could invest the same $2.5M to expand a regional rare-disease program, which modeling suggests would provide multidisciplinary clinics, care coordination, subsidized medications, home nursing support, and therapy services to about 40 children in the region (including several with ATAD1), likely improving symptom control, reducing crisis visits, and enhancing ongoing care for many families; choosing this would preclude offering the gene therapy slot to this infant this year. The infant’s parents strongly request the gene therapy and are prepared to advocate publicly, while the treating clinicians, rare-disease program director, and the hospital philanthropy/allocation committee are deeply divided. What should the hospital philanthropy/allocation committee do?
Choice A: Use the $2.5M to expand the regional rare-disease program, providing multidisciplinary care and subsidies to many children (the infant will not receive the gene therapy now).
Choice B: Use the $2.5M to fund the single compassionate-use gene-replacement therapy slot and treat this infant now.

A maternal-fetal medicine physician is caring for a 28-year-old pregnant woman at 19 weeks’ gestation whose prior child died in infancy from SMOC1-related microphthalmia with limb anomalies, and current fetal testing confirms the same pathogenic variant with severe anomalies already visible on ultrasound. A one-time prenatal intervention is available only through a single hospital slot this month; it is extraordinarily expensive, supported by a limited charity reserve, and the team knows that using it here would likely prevent another similarly affected child from receiving the only available slot this quarter. The mother is alert, oriented, and consistently requests the intervention for this pregnancy, but she cannot accurately explain the treatment’s limits and has not fully grasped that the resource is being rationed among patients with comparable need. The treating physician must decide whether to proceed with the intervention for this fetus or reserve the slot for another child with the same rare condition who is waiting for access. What should the treating maternal-fetal medicine physician and rare-disease genetics team do?
Choice A: Proceed with the prenatal intervention for this fetus.
Choice B: Reserve the slot for another child waiting for access.
