A 29-year-old pregnant woman at 18 weeks’ gestation is carrying a fetus found on prenatal sequencing to have biallelic pathogenic GPX4 variants, with ultrasound showing severe skeletal dysplasia, a narrow chest, delayed ossification, platyspondyly, rhizomelic shortening, and evolving respiratory insufficiency consistent with spondylometaphyseal dysplasia, Sedaghatian type. The fetal therapy program has one remaining slot this month for an invasive prenatal protocol that requires repeated monitoring, specialized staff, and a large share of limited research funding; if this fetus is enrolled, another fetus with a different rare disorder and a stronger chance of producing interpretable data will be turned away. The mother is alert, fully capable of decision-making, and after detailed counseling she consistently requests the intervention for this fetus, saying she understands the prognosis is grave and the benefit is uncertain but wants every reasonable chance to try. The selection committee must decide whether to use the last slot for this pregnancy or reserve it for the other candidate. What should the fetal therapy selection committee and treating physician do?
Choice A: Enroll this pregnancy in the prenatal protocol.
Choice B: Reserve the last protocol slot for the other candidate.

A 6-year-old boy with confirmed GPC4-related Keipert syndrome has cognitive impairment, broad thumbs and halluces, hoarse voice, facial differences, and congenital cardiovascular abnormalities, and his parents have spent years learning the disorder in detail because specialty care is scarce where they live. A publicly funded hospital program has one available slot for an expensive investigational treatment that has only limited data in Keipert syndrome, and the boy’s parents can accurately explain the diagnosis, the uncertainties, and the practical burdens of treatment, but they insist that his access should be prioritized because their family has already traveled repeatedly for care and he is now showing worsening feeding and cardiac issues. The same slot could instead go to another child with the same disorder who has far fewer specialty resources locally and whose family has waited longer for access under the program’s published criteria, even though the evidence does not clearly show which child is more likely to benefit. The treating metabolic geneticist must decide whether to honor the parents’ fact-based request for priority or apply the program’s equal-access rule strictly so the scarce publicly subsidized slot is distributed in the same way for both children. What should the treating metabolic geneticist do?
Choice A: Prioritize this child’s application based on the parents’ fact-based request.
Choice B: Apply the program’s equal-access rule and do not prioritize this child’s application.

An 8-month-old infant has progressive generalized myoclonic and bilateral tonic-clonic seizures, emerging ataxia, severe developmental delay, and metabolic instability; genetic testing confirmed biallelic pathogenic variants in ALDH5A1 consistent with succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency. A newly available one-time AAV-based gene replacement therapy has shown promising early results but carries uncertain long-term benefit and a small risk of catastrophic immune-mediated liver failure; administering it outside a trial requires a $2.1M hospital subsidy. The infant’s parents, after repeated counseling and review of available data, demonstrate clear factual understanding of the therapy’s potential benefits, uncertainties, and risks and explicitly request the treatment for their child; the clinical team agrees that denying the therapy would likely worsen the child’s prognosis. The hospital’s Rare Therapies Fund can support only one such individualized subsidy per year, and three other children on the institutional waitlist need similarly costly one-time subsidies this year; the allocation committee is sharply divided because approving this case would exhaust the fund and prevent comparable access for those other children. What should the hospital rare-disease treatment allocation committee and medical director do?
Choice A: Approve and allocate the one-time gene replacement therapy for this infant using the Rare Therapies Fund.
Choice B: Decline allocation of the gene therapy and provide best-available standard supportive and symptomatic care while preserving the fund for future cases.

A 7-year-old child with biallelic pathogenic GBA1 variants has Gaucher disease–ophthalmoplegia–cardiovascular calcification syndrome, experiencing progressive gait disturbance, oculomotor apraxia, thrombocytopenia with recurrent epistaxis, sensorineural hearing impairment, pulmonary fibrosis, and worsening aortic and mitral valve calcification despite intensive supportive and enzyme-directed care. A university rare-disease program has one remaining publicly and philanthropically funded manufacturing slot this year for an individualized GBA1-targeted gene-modifying therapy; the therapy has a plausible but unproven chance of slowing progression, and its risks are serious but considered medically acceptable by the treating specialists. The program cannot expand capacity this cycle, and using the slot for this child would definitively prevent several other rare-disease platform candidates from receiving development and treatment opportunities that the review group estimates may produce greater combined benefit. Committee members disagree about how much weight to give the child’s urgent risk of irreversible cardiac and pulmonary decline versus the program’s responsibility to use scarce manufacturing, regulatory, and clinical resources where they are expected to help more patients overall. What should the hospital rare-disease allocation committee do?
Choice A: Authorize the individualized GBA1-targeted therapy slot for this child.
Choice B: Decline the individualized therapy slot and continue intensive conventional/supportive management while preserving the slot for higher-yield platform cases.

A 32-year-old man with autosomal dominant striatal neurodegeneration from a pathogenic PDE8B variant is alert, fully informed, and still working, but over the past year he has developed progressive rigidity, bradykinesia, impaired rapid alternating movements, and recurrent falls from worsening gait disturbance. His family has secured outside philanthropic funding for a personalized PDE8B-directed RNA-silencing therapy, but the hospital would still need to provide its only neurogenetics precision-therapy bed, specialized pharmacy preparation, intensive neurologic monitoring, and six weeks of inpatient staffing because no outpatient or lower-acuity pathway exists. An external expert panel agrees that the treatment has uncertain but plausible disease-modifying benefit and similar procedural risk whether given now or later, but estimates that a several-month delay could leave him permanently dependent for ambulation if his current rate of decline continues. The next available slot is reserved under the hospital’s policy for rare neurogenetic patients with rapidly life-threatening deterioration and no temporizing option; using it for him would postpone at least two such admissions for months, during which those patients face substantial risk of irreversible organ or neurologic collapse. His treating neurologist argues that this may be his last realistic opportunity to preserve independent walking, while the hospital rare-disease allocation committee is concerned that a privately funded exception would move a less immediately endangered patient ahead of patients in greater medical need. What should the hospital rare-disease allocation committee do?
Choice A: Grant an exception and admit him now for the personalized PDE8B-directed therapy.
Choice B: Defer admission until he meets the program’s need-based priority criteria or a later slot becomes available.

A 9-year-old boy with congenital RPGR-associated achromatopsia has experienced significant visual impairment since infancy, including pendular nystagmus, high myopia, reduced visual acuity, abnormal color testing, central scotomas, foveal hypoplasia, retinal pigment epithelial mottling, and an undetectable light-adapted electroretinogram, despite receiving optimized low-vision and school supports. His clinicians have identified a compassionate-use retinal gene-augmentation protocol that could potentially preserve useful central vision, though the benefit is uncertain; the protocol requires subretinal surgery, immune suppression, prolonged monitoring, and a hospital subsidy equivalent to the entire discretionary access fund of the rare-eye program for the year. No alternative funding is available, and using the fund for this protocol would mean cancelling or deferring genetic testing, low-vision devices, mobility training, travel assistance, and care coordination for many other rare retinal disease patients who otherwise cannot obtain those services. The hospital gene-therapy review committee and rare-eye program leadership are responsible for deciding on exceptional subsidies and agree that the child is an eligible candidate, that the expected benefit is uncertain, and that the case could provide practical information for future RPGR treatment planning. Approving the subsidy would focus the shared fund on one high-impact, uncertain intervention, while declining it would preserve access to essential services for many patients but likely end this child’s only realistic chance to receive the protocol. What should the hospital gene-therapy review committee and rare-eye program leadership do?
Choice A: Approve the subsidized compassionate-use RPGR retinal gene-augmentation protocol for this child.
Choice B: Decline the subsidy and reserve the rare-eye access fund for essential services available to many rare retinal disease patients.

A 34-year-old woman with biallelic pathogenic PSAP variants has adult-onset metachromatic leukodystrophy with progressive difficulty walking, hyporeflexia, slowed nerve conduction, optic atrophy, emotional lability, depression, and worsening memory impairment, but she remains alert, oriented, and able to explain her diagnosis and options in detail. There is no established disease-modifying therapy available to her, and an academic center has offered a one-time compassionate-use intrathecal gene-replacement protocol with limited human evidence, uncertain chance of slowing progression, and serious but not clearly prohibitive risks; her treating specialists agree that either pursuing or declining it would be clinically defensible. She consistently requests the protocol, accurately describes the limited evidence, possible complications, lack of long-term outcome data, and how those uncertainties apply to her current neurologic decline, and explains that even a modest chance of preserving mobility and communication is worth the burdens to her. The hospital’s capped rare-disease assistance fund cannot be expanded this year, and paying for this single intervention would use nearly all remaining funds that otherwise would provide the same fixed subsidy to eight uninsured rare-disease patients for approved enzyme replacement, nutritional support, seizure medications, mobility equipment, or home nursing that they cannot otherwise obtain. The hospital rare-disease funding committee has previously used this fixed-subsidy rule to avoid allowing any one ultra-costly request to exhaust the shared fund, but it must now decide whether to make an exception for her requested intervention or apply the rule. What should the hospital rare-disease funding committee do?
Choice A: Approve charity funding for the compassionate-use PSAP gene-replacement protocol.
Choice B: Deny charity funding and apply the fixed-subsidy rare-disease funding rule.

A 17-year-old with genetically confirmed 2p21 microdeletion syndrome involving PPM1B has experienced seizures, cystinuria, recurrent hypocalcemia, growth delay, hypernasal speech, global developmental delay, and mitochondrial respiratory-chain dysfunction since infancy, and now has several metabolic decompensations each year despite optimized rare-disease supportive care. His metabolic genetics and neurology teams estimate that, without a disease-modifying option, he is likely to experience gradual loss of communication, mobility, and school participation over the next 1–3 years, with intermittent hospitalizations and a meaningful possibility of longer survival with substantial disability. A university group offers a one-time personalized intrathecal molecular therapy under compassionate-use oversight, funded outside the hospital’s treatment budget and not taking another patient’s slot, with limited preclinical data suggesting possible stabilization but no human efficacy data and a credible risk of fatal neuroinflammation, permanent worsening of seizures, or loss of his remaining speech and interaction. The patient is alert and oriented, and separate evaluations by adolescent medicine, psychology, neurology, genetics, and ethics conclude that he consistently understands the uncertainties, compares the possible outcomes in his own words, resists minor reframing of the decision, and explains that even a small chance of preserving communication and independence is worth the possibility of a shorter or worse life. The hospital compassionate-use committee must decide whether to permit the intervention when the treating team is divided between honoring his sustained reasoning and avoiding a medically caused catastrophe in someone who may still have meaningful time with supportive care. What should the hospital compassionate-use committee do?
Choice A: Authorize the personalized intrathecal therapy under compassionate-use monitoring
Choice B: Decline authorization and continue optimized supportive and palliative-directed rare-disease care

disease: Junctional epidermolysis bullosa with pyloric atresia
vignette:
A 9-day-old newborn with biallelic pathogenic ITGA6 variants has junctional epidermolysis bullosa with congenital pyloric atresia, widespread skin and oral mucosal blistering, recurrent skin infections, early renal dysplasia with hematuria, and urethral stricture. The regional children’s hospital has one remaining opening this quarter in its specialized epidermolysis bullosa surgical ICU pathway, which offers coordinated gastrointestinal and urologic surgery, intensive wound and infection-control nursing, and access to a charity-funded epithelial-cell support program whose benefit in this genotype is uncertain and whose first-year costs are expected to exceed $1 million. The infant is the sickest current referral and local clinicians believe transfer could reduce the risk of infection, surgical complications, and prolonged organ injury, but the referring NICU can still provide parenteral nutrition, staged pyloric and urologic procedures, infection management, and telemedicine-guided wound care with a plausible though less supported path through the next several months. Approving admission would use the pathway’s last slot and most of a supplemental fund that, by policy, is meant to cover transport, genetic testing, lodging, and initial specialty treatment for an estimated four to six rare-disease infants from rural, uninsured, and historically under-resourced families expected before the next funding cycle in five months. The hospital’s rare-disease allocation committee, which is responsible for applying both severity-based and access-barrier criteria when distributing the pathway’s limited funds, must decide whether to use the remaining opening for this newborn now or preserve the fund for those anticipated referrals. What should the hospital rare-disease allocation committee do?
Choice A: Approve immediate admission to the specialized epidermolysis bullosa surgical ICU pathway with access to the charity-funded epithelial-cell support program.
Choice B: Do not approve the specialized pathway admission now, and continue maximal local NICU-based care with telemedicine support while preserving the supplemental fund for anticipated under-resourced rare-disease referrals.

A 7-week-old infant with Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome, caused by a de novo pathogenic SKI variant, presents with severe failure to thrive, ventriculomegaly, micrognathia with intermittent airway obstruction, joint hyperflexibility, inguinal and umbilical hernias, arachnodactyly, and early mitral regurgitation. Standard supportive care is expected to require intensive nutrition, airway monitoring, cardiac surveillance, and staged surgeries, but the infant's neurologic and cardiovascular prognosis is unpredictable and there is no established disease-modifying treatment. A nonprofit academic group can develop a personalized SKI-silencing treatment to reduce expression of the mutant gene copy; independent reviewers find the expected benefit uncertain but potentially meaningful, and the safety risks serious but not clearly prohibitive. The hospital’s rare-disease therapeutics committee has one bespoke-therapy slot and one pooled precision-medicine budget this year, and funding this program would use nearly all of the budget that otherwise supports genomic diagnosis, care coordination, adaptive equipment, nutrition support, and conventional therapies for about 35 other children with rare disorders. The infant’s program would also generate manufacturing, dosing, and safety data that could accelerate future treatments for children with SKI-related disease and related TGF-beta pathway disorders, while preserving the pooled budget would maintain more even access to rare-disease services this year. What should the hospital rare-disease therapeutics committee do?
Choice A: Authorize and fund the personalized SKI-silencing therapy-development pathway for this infant.
Choice B: Decline the bespoke therapy-development pathway and preserve the pooled budget for broadly available rare-disease services and treatments.

A 7-month-old girl with a de novo pathogenic ATP6V1B2 variant has congenital profound bilateral sensorineural hearing impairment, absent fingernails and thumbnails, hypoplastic toenails, oligodontia, early dental anomalies, and dolichocephaly consistent with autosomal dominant deafness-onychodystrophy syndrome. Her parents rely on Medicaid and hospital charity support and ask the hospital’s rare-disease program to use its only subsidized personalized inner-ear gene-editing production slot this year for her before the early language-development window narrows. The proposed therapy is biologically plausible but has no ATP6V1B2-specific outcome data, uncertain durability, unknown long-term inner-ear and neurologic risks, and would still require intensive audiology follow-up; cochlear implantation with developmental and communication support is also available and considered a medically reasonable care pathway. If the slot is used for her, the program must cancel two scheduled rare-disease platform manufacturing runs involving six children with different progressive genetic disorders, for whom the shared protocol is expected to produce more generalizable safety and dosing data and a greater aggregate chance of measurable benefit. The allocation committee is being pressed by the infant’s parents, who see this as her only chance at a potentially biologic hearing intervention, while program leaders warn that choosing her case may substantially reduce what the same scarce funds, manufacturing time, and specialist effort can achieve for the broader rare-disease program. What should the hospital rare-disease advanced-therapy allocation committee do?
Choice A: Use the subsidized personalized ATP6V1B2 inner-ear gene-editing production slot for the infant now.
Choice B: Preserve the production slot for the scheduled rare-disease platform runs and proceed with cochlear implantation plus intensive developmental and audiologic support for the infant.

A 34-year-old woman with a pathogenic AXIN2 variant and AXIN2-related polyposis has dozens of adenomatous colonic polyps and a rectal adenoma with high-grade dysplasia. She is alert, well-informed, and clinically eligible for either of two accepted cancer-prevention pathways with comparable expected cancer control in her case: total proctocolectomy, which is resource-efficient but carries substantial risks of infertility, sexual dysfunction, chronic bowel dysfunction, and prolonged work loss, or a year-long organ-preserving program of serial advanced endoscopic resections and close surveillance, which may delay or avoid surgery but requires repeated anesthesia-supported procedures. The hospital’s hereditary cancer program has a fixed pool of advanced endoscopy time reserved for complex rare-disease cases, and approving this pathway would use approximately the same capacity needed for 6 to 8 shorter cancer-prevention procedures for other safety-net patients with hereditary gastrointestinal cancer syndromes. The committee agrees that neither pathway is medically inappropriate, but it cannot both make the individualized organ-preserving option realistically accessible for this patient and preserve the same procedural capacity for the larger group of patients awaiting lower-intensity preventive care. What should the hospital rare-disease access committee do?
Choice A: Approve the intensive organ-preserving endoscopic management pathway.
Choice B: Decline the intensive pathway and offer standard risk-reducing proctocolectomy with routine postoperative support.

An 8-year-old girl with a pathogenic BTNL2 variant has severe early-onset sarcoidosis with progressive pulmonary fibrosis, recurrent pneumothorax, vision-threatening uveitis and glaucoma, declining liver function with hepatomegaly, hypercalcemia, anemia, and painful arthritis despite standard immunosuppressive options. Her rare-disease team can request a one-time personalized immune-reset protocol using autologous gene-edited hematopoietic cells, but experience is limited to a few biologically related cases; the chance of stabilizing her disease is real but uncertain, and the treatment carries substantial risk of fatal inflammatory toxicity, prolonged ICU dependence, or permanent neurologic injury. Providing the protocol would use the hospital’s only pediatric ICU-supported cellular-therapy slot for several months and most of a non-expandable state rare-disease emergency fund that is also being used to support other children with severe rare disorders, including some needing time-sensitive enzyme replacement starts, transplant-bridging support, or urgent molecular therapies not otherwise funded. If the protocol is not authorized, she would continue best available noncurative care, which may lessen inflammation and symptoms but is not expected to reliably prevent further lung, liver, and eye damage. The hospital rare-disease allocation committee must decide whether to commit the scarce slot and emergency funds to this child now or preserve them for other seriously ill children with urgent rare-disease needs. What should the hospital rare-disease allocation committee do?
Choice A: Authorize the personalized immune-reset protocol for this child now.
Choice B: Decline authorization for the protocol and continue best available noncurative care while preserving the scarce slot and emergency funds.

A 7-month-old boy with sclerosteosis due to biallelic pathogenic SOST variants is experiencing rapidly progressive craniofacial hyperostosis, narrowing around the optic canals and posterior fossa, worsening sensorineural hearing impairment, facial nerve weakness, ptosis, abnormal nasal morphology, tall stature, and 2-3 finger syndactyly. His hospital has one publicly subsidized individualized molecular-therapy slot this year for rare skeletal dysplasias; the treatment is not proven to prevent long-term disability, but there is no clearly superior alternative, and both immediate enrollment and short deferral with close surveillance are considered medically defensible. The program requires prolonged admission, repeated anesthesia-supported imaging, ICU backup, interpreter-supported education, and years of standardized follow-up data, and its external funder has stated that renewal will depend on complete safety reporting from this year’s treated case after a prior rare-disease platform lost funding when a high-risk enrollment produced incomplete follow-up after a serious complication. The child’s family lives far from the tertiary center and has missed visits because Medicaid transportation approvals, insurance reauthorizations, and interpreter scheduling have repeatedly failed, but the parents have completed all education sessions, accurately explain the risks and monitoring plan, and are asking to proceed before hearing, facial nerve function, or vision is permanently lost. Approving him now would require using much of the program’s annual housing, navigation, interpreter, ICU-reserve, and research-coordination budget for this single admission, while deferring him for a time-limited readiness period would require the family to demonstrate reliable attendance under a system that has already created many of the barriers to care. What should the hospital individualized-therapy program committee do?
Choice A: Approve the child for the individualized therapy program now with hospital-funded transportation, housing, interpreter services, ICU backup, and intensive care coordination.
Choice B: Defer enrollment for a time-limited readiness period with funded transportation trials, interpreter-supported visits, standard surveillance, and neurosurgical/ENT interventions as needed.

A 19-year-old college student with biallelic pathogenic UNC93B1 variants has survived two episodes of herpes simplex encephalitis and remains at risk of another severe neurologic relapse despite suppressive acyclovir and an emergency admission plan. She is alert, oriented, and, over multiple meetings, consistently explains that an experimental autologous gene-corrected hematopoietic stem-cell procedure has limited evidence for her condition, uncertain durability, and a 15–25% estimated risk of treatment-related death or severe permanent morbidity, while standard preventive care also leaves a meaningful risk of future encephalitis with loss of speech, independence, or ventilator dependence. Her immunology, infectious disease, neurology, and transplant teams agree that continuing standard preventive care and pursuing the experimental procedure are both medically defensible, because neither pathway offers a clearly superior chance of preserving long-term survival or communication. The procedure would require a one-time $2 million allocation from the hospital’s rare-disease charity fund, whose annual budget is $6 million and whose current commitments include antiviral prophylaxis, emergency transfers, genetic testing, and specialty access for about 60 uninsured rare-disease patients; approving this request would require deferring or denying a substantial portion of those services this year and would likely set the same funding threshold for future similarly costly individualized requests. After several ethics consultations, she continues to give a coherent and stable explanation that the possibility of preventing another encephalitis episode is worth the treatment risk to her, and the hospital rare-disease funding committee must decide whether to authorize the expenditure. What should the hospital rare-disease funding committee do?
Choice A: Approve charity funding for the experimental gene-corrected stem-cell procedure.
Choice B: Decline charity funding for the experimental procedure and continue suppressive antiviral care with rapid emergency-treatment planning.

A 31-year-old pregnant woman at 23 weeks’ gestation carries a male fetus with a pathogenic FLNA variant causing otopalatodigital syndrome type 2, with imaging showing a markedly narrow chest, abnormal ribs, bowed long bones, fibular aplasia, large fontanelles, cleft palate, hearing-related structural abnormalities, and evolving cardiac valve and septal abnormalities. Her prior son died in infancy from the same condition after prolonged ventilation and multiple surgeries; she is alert, oriented, and accurately explains that the proposed individualized prenatal allele-silencing treatment has only laboratory and animal support, uncertain relevance to this fetus’s variant, and risks including fetal demise, neurodevelopmental injury, and worsening cardiac disease. The hospital has one donor-funded manufacturing and fetal-procedure slot this year: using it for this fetus under expanded-access oversight would provide a single customized attempt outside a formal trial, while preserving it would allow a planned FLNA fetal-therapy platform study to enroll several future pregnancies and generate dosing and safety data needed for broader access. The fetal therapy board is responsible both for responding to this family’s factually informed request in a pregnancy likely to result in death or profound disability without disease-modifying therapy, and for stewarding a scarce program whose funding and scientific momentum may be lost if the platform study is cancelled. What should the fetal therapy board do?
Choice A: Offer the individualized prenatal allele-silencing intervention under expanded-access oversight.
Choice B: Decline the individualized intervention and preserve the slot, funding, and manufacturing capacity for the planned FLNA platform study.

A 6-month-old boy with encephalocraniocutaneous lipomatosis from a mosaic pathogenic KRAS variant has refractory seizures, recurrent ventriculomegaly requiring neurosurgical drainage, worsening visual impairment from corneal and retinal disease, hypertonia, craniofacial overgrowth, and profound developmental delay. His parents strongly request a one-patient compassionate-use intrathecal KRAS-targeted antisense therapy being developed for related mosaic RAS-pathway disorders, arguing that continued supportive care will only watch their child lose neurologic function while a possible treatment window closes. The treating neurogenetics team agrees that further brain injury may soon become irreversible, but no infant with this condition has received the therapy, and the limited preclinical data leave uncertain risks of neuroinflammation, vascular injury, immune reactions, worsening seizures, and disruption of developing brain tissue. Supportive care could continue with shunting, antiseizure therapy, feeding support, visual care, and repeated hospitalization, but it would not target the KRAS-driven disease process. The hospital innovative therapeutics committee must decide whether authorizing a first-in-condition intervention is justified when inaction may permit irreversible decline, while action may itself cause severe neurologic injury or death. What should the hospital innovative therapeutics committee do?
Choice A: Authorize compassionate-use intrathecal KRAS-targeted therapy now.
Choice B: Do not authorize the experimental KRAS-targeted therapy; continue supportive and symptom-directed care.

A 6-week-old infant on Medicaid with biallelic pathogenic TSPOAP1 variants has presented since birth with feeding difficulty, excessive salivation, rigidity, brisk lower-limb reflexes, postural tremor, limb dystonia, and early motor delay; an older sibling with the same disorder is now tube-fed and has recurrent hospitalizations for fever-triggered dystonic crises. The hospital’s rare-disease therapeutics program has one remaining manufacturing slot this year for a personalized intracerebroventricular TSPOAP1 gene-replacement construct, with limited compassionate-use and animal data suggesting a plausible chance of meaningful neurologic benefit if given in infancy, but with uncertain durability and incompletely characterized risks. Using the slot for this infant would consume several million dollars, most of the center’s vector-production capacity, and specialized regulatory staff for 9 to 12 months, postponing a platform protocol projected to enroll 25 to 40 children with severe rare neurologic diseases and delaying the data needed to expand access beyond single-patient treatments. The family lives several hours from the center, has limited English proficiency, and previously missed appointments when transportation and interpreter services were not arranged; the care team believes participation is feasible only with intensive interpreter, lodging, transport, care-coordination, and emergency-response support that would draw from the same limited rare-disease program budget. The hospital genomic therapeutics committee must decide whether to authorize individualized treatment now, accepting the diversion of scarce program capacity, or preserve the slot for the broader platform program while offering the infant optimized symptomatic treatment, registry enrollment, and later trial consideration despite the possibility of irreversible progression during the delay. What should the hospital genomic therapeutics committee do?
Choice A: Approve immediate individualized TSPOAP1 gene-replacement therapy with intensive logistical, interpreter, and follow-up support.
Choice B: Defer individualized therapy and provide optimized symptomatic treatment, registry enrollment, and future trial consideration while preserving the manufacturing slot for the broader rare-disease platform program.

A 29-year-old pregnant woman at 22 weeks’ gestation is carrying a fetus with biallelic pathogenic PEX6 variants causing autosomal recessive spinocerebellar ataxia-blindness-deafness syndrome; her older child has the same rare disorder, with childhood-onset gait ataxia, optic atrophy, sensorimotor neuropathy, cochlear degeneration, head tremor, and progressive loss of independent walking despite extensive supportive care. Because neurologic injury in this condition is thought to begin before or soon after birth and there is no established disease-modifying postnatal treatment, a rare-disease consortium has obtained limited permission for a one-time in-utero PEX6-targeted vector infusion, with the hospital required to independently approve any fetal procedure that may cause fetal death or permanent developmental injury even when the pregnant patient gives informed consent. Consultants agree that the chance of benefit is unknown but biologically plausible, and that the procedure could also cause fetal demise, severe inflammatory liver injury, preterm delivery, or irreversible injury to developing tissues before the child can experience any possible benefit. The mother is alert and oriented, has completed repeated counseling with genetics, maternal-fetal medicine, neonatology, and ethics teams, accurately explains the uncertainties and catastrophic risks, and consistently says that, after caring for one affected child, she would accept a substantial fetal procedural risk to try to prevent the same decline. Experienced members of the oversight committee disagree about whether approving the only pre-symptomatic intervention gives appropriate weight to her sustained reasoning or whether their mandate requires them to withhold authorization for a procedure that may itself inflict profound harm on a highly vulnerable fetus. What should the hospital fetal intervention oversight committee do?
Choice A: Authorize the single-patient in-utero PEX6-targeted vector infusion.
Choice B: Decline authorization and continue prenatal monitoring with delivery planning and postnatal supportive or investigational care.

A 34-year-old woman with genetically confirmed CTSK-related pycnodysostosis experiences recurrent disabling fractures, severe scoliosis, obstructive sleep apnea from craniofacial narrowing, micrognathia, chronic jaw complications, and increasing dependence on caregivers despite expert multidisciplinary care. She is alert and oriented, and has spent two years working with her rare-bone-disease team, an advocacy group, and academic scientists to evaluate a personalized experimental CTSK gene-correction protocol available only through a hospital-sponsored compassionate-use pathway; the protocol has no established success rate in pycnodysostosis, but the team agrees it is medically plausible, not futile, and carries serious risks including uncontrolled bone remodeling, airway swelling, infertility, or death. The treatment requires a single upfront institutional payment that cannot be reduced, shared, or externally supplemented, and approving it would use nearly the entire annual philanthropic fund that otherwise provides fixed-size grants to many rare-disease patients for genetic diagnoses, travel to specialty centers, mobility and airway devices, and otherwise inaccessible treatments. The fund’s written rules prohibit individualized exceptions because the committee has committed to distributing support evenly, yet the patient gives a detailed, consistent explanation of why she accepts the uncertainties and catastrophic risks, why continued supportive care no longer fits her long-term goals, and why she would make the same choice even if the treatment failed. The hospital rare-disease therapeutics committee must decide whether to approve the one-patient funding exception or follow the equal-access funding rule. What should the hospital rare-disease therapeutics committee do?
Choice A: Approve funding and access for the personalized experimental CTSK gene-correction protocol.
Choice B: Deny the individualized funding request and continue standard multidisciplinary management under the equal-access funding policy.

disease: Combined immunodeficiency due to DOCK8 deficiency
vignette:
A 3-year-old boy with biallelic pathogenic DOCK8 variants has combined immunodeficiency with B lymphocytopenia, recurrent pneumonias and sinusitis, chronic otitis media, recurrent candida and viral infections, extensive verrucae, recurrent bacterial skin infections with ulceration, and a recently resected early squamous cell carcinoma. His immunology, oncology, and transplant teams agree that allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the only potentially curative treatment, but outside experts reviewing his case are divided: some believe proceeding now is justified because further infection or cancer recurrence could permanently close his window for cure, while others believe his active viral skin disease, frailty, and cancer history make his expected transplant benefit uncertain compared with other candidates. The regional publicly funded rare-immunodeficiency transplant program has one remaining intensive pathway this quarter, including unrelated-donor procurement, specialized isolation nursing, and a capped charitable fund that covers unreimbursed transplant costs; no additional pathway can be opened until the next funding cycle. The program’s allocation framework usually reserves these pathways for candidates expected to gain the greatest aggregate survival benefit from scarce staff time, donor logistics, and public funds, but applying that framework here would mean asking one of the sickest children in the program to wait despite a plausible risk that delay will make curative treatment impossible. The transplant committee must decide whether to make an exception and offer the pathway now or follow the usual allocation framework and defer him while providing maximal antimicrobial, nutritional, dermatologic, and oncologic support. What should the regional rare-immunodeficiency transplant committee do?
Choice A: Offer the publicly funded transplant pathway now as an exception to the usual allocation framework.
Choice B: Defer transplant until the next funding cycle while continuing maximal medical and oncologic management under the usual allocation framework.

A 16-year-old with genetically confirmed Kindler epidermolysis bullosa from biallelic FERMT1 variants has experienced severe skin blistering since birth, progressive photosensitivity, poikiloderma, recurrent infected wounds, dysphagia from mucosal scarring, chronic colitis with anemia, severe periodontitis with tooth loss, and urethral squamous dysplasia requiring close cancer surveillance. Despite intensive wound care, nutrition support, antibiotics, endoscopic dilations, and malignancy monitoring, the patient has had repeated admissions for infection and nutritional decline, and the treating team estimates that irreversible deterioration or death is likely within 12–18 months without a major change in management. The hospital can offer a single-patient institutional protocol using autologous gene-corrected epidermal stem-cell sheets for selected skin and mucosal surfaces; the approach is biologically plausible, but experience in Kindler epidermolysis bullosa is extremely limited, and serious complications such as graft failure, overwhelming infection, procedure-related death, or later tumor formation are possible. The protocol would use nearly all of the hospital’s annual public and philanthropic personalized-medicine budget and its only available GMP manufacturing slot, delaying by at least two years a broader inherited-skin-disease platform expected to enroll dozens of future rare-disease patients and generate evidence for multiple conditions. The hospital’s rare-disease therapeutics committee is divided between authorizing the individualized protocol now and preserving the same resources for the broader program. What should the hospital rare-disease therapeutics committee do?
Choice A: Approve the individualized FERMT1 gene-corrected autologous grafting protocol for this patient now.
Choice B: Decline the individualized protocol and continue intensive standard care while preserving funds and manufacturing capacity for the broader inherited-skin-disease platform.

A 6-year-old girl with a pathogenic DDX3X variant has severe generalized hypotonia, dyskinesias, cortical dysplasia, microcephaly, autistic behavior with intermittent aggression, and vision and hearing impairment; over the past year she has lost several functional communication skills despite intensive supportive care. The hospital has opened a first-in-human personalized antisense therapy pathway, and this year it has funding for only one non-expandable wraparound support slot covering inpatient monitoring, genetic counseling, interpreter-supported consent, transportation, lodging, and intensive care coordination that insurance will not cover. She meets the same medical eligibility criteria as the other candidates, and the rare-disease neurologists agree that the likely benefit, burdens, and risks are comparably uncertain across candidates; however, postponing enrollment for 6 to 9 months could mean further loss of communication and behavioral stability for her. Several other eligible children in the program have greater immediate medical need, including rapidly progressive loss of ambulation or declining ventilatory reserve, and the committee has been told that a similar delay could close a meaningful treatment window for one of them; unlike this family, however, those families have English fluency, stable housing, and some ability to complete travel, monitoring, and research requirements without the full support package. Her parents are recent immigrants with limited English literacy, unstable housing, and no realistic way to self-fund or coordinate the pathway without the slot, and the committee knows that its decision will shape whether similarly situated families trust that the program is reachable for them. What should the hospital rare-disease access committee do?
Choice A: Assign the hospital-funded wraparound support slot to this child’s DDX3X antisense therapy pathway now.
Choice B: Do not assign the support slot to her now, reserving it for an eligible child with greater immediate medical deterioration.

disease: Severe neonatal hypotonia-seizures-encephalopathy syndrome due to 5q31.3 microdeletion
vignette:
A 29-year-old pregnant woman at 23 weeks’ gestation has fetal testing showing a pathogenic 5q31.3 microdeletion involving PURA, the same rare disorder that caused her first child to develop severe muscular hypotonia, feeding failure, respiratory distress, focal tonic seizures with abnormal EEG, severe developmental impairment, and progressive brain atrophy beginning in infancy. A fetal-therapy program has one manufacturer-supplied dose of an intra-amniotic PURA gene-replacement product available under regulator-reviewed compassionate use before 24 weeks; the intervention has plausible disease-model support and has passed toxicity review, but there are no human PURA fetal-treatment outcomes, and known risks include fetal death, immune-mediated neurologic injury, preterm labor, maternal complications, and loss of future trial eligibility if serious harm occurs. The woman is alert, oriented, and has met separately with genetics, maternal-fetal medicine, neonatology, anesthesia, an independent ethics consultant, and an outside PURA researcher; she accurately explains that benefit is uncertain, that the fetus is not yet symptomatic, that standard care would focus on seizure, respiratory, and feeding support after birth, and that she is willing to accept a substantial risk of fetal loss or maternal complication to try to prevent the untreated neurologic course she has already witnessed. The committee agrees there is a narrow biological rationale for acting before birth and no established prenatal alternative, but its members would be directly initiating an irreversible, poorly validated procedure in a patient who is not medically unstable and whose fetus may be harmed by the attempt. The fetal-therapy committee must decide whether to authorize the one-time compassionate-use infusion now or decline to provide it while continuing standard prenatal and neonatal planning. What should the fetal-therapy committee do?
Choice A: Authorize the compassionate-use fetal PURA gene-replacement infusion.
Choice B: Decline to provide the fetal intervention and continue standard prenatal and neonatal supportive planning.

An 18-year-old woman with childhood-onset KCNQ1OT1-related isolated hemihyperplasia has facial asymmetry, progressive hemihypertrophy, severe scoliosis after multiple operations, impaired pain sensation with recurrent injuries, mild intellectual disability, abnormal dentition, and lifelong tumor surveillance because her future course is uncertain. A rare-disease center can provide a compassionate-use epigenetic silencing infusion for related imprinting disorders; a small number of patients with adjacent conditions have received it under monitoring, but there is no reliable outcome data for her condition, and experts disagree about whether the possibility of slowing progression justifies the poorly quantifiable risk of irreversible neurologic injury, infertility, malignant transformation, or death. She is alert and oriented, and after repeated meetings with genetics, neurology, oncology, rehabilitation, and ethics consultants, she consistently explains the uncertain benefit, the lack of disease-specific evidence, the potential for permanent or life-ending harm, and why she would rather accept those risks than continue with progressive deformity, injury precautions, operations, and surveillance. Her clinicians agree that her mild intellectual disability does not impair her ability to understand and reason through this decision, but the treating rare-disease physician must decide whether providing the infusion would cross a line from respecting a carefully reasoned request into causing an avoidable serious harm. What should the treating rare-disease physician do?
Choice A: Proceed with the compassionate-use epigenetic silencing infusion under the approved monitoring protocol.
Choice B: Decline to administer the infusion and continue tumor surveillance, orthopedic care, injury prevention, rehabilitation, and supportive management.

A 3-month-old infant with biallelic pathogenic RNU4ATAC variants has congenital-onset Lowry-Wood syndrome, presenting with microcephaly, nystagmus with early retinal pigment changes, severe short stature, delayed skeletal maturation, irregular epiphyses, coxa vara, and recurrent feeding-related respiratory decompensations requiring prolonged hospital care. A personalized intrathecal RNA therapy has been manufactured for her specific spliceosomal defect; cell and animal models show correction of the molecular abnormality and suggest the best chance of preserving vision and neurodevelopment is within the next month, but no child has received this agent and the independent safety review estimates a non-trivial risk of fatal neuroinflammation, seizures, accelerated retinal injury, or permanent neurologic worsening. Without the therapy, the team expects active supportive care to reduce suffering and manage respiratory, feeding, orthopedic, visual, and developmental complications, but it is not expected to prevent progressive disability, painful skeletal deterioration, vision loss, repeated admissions, and lifelong dependence on complex care. Because administering the drug would create an irreversible first-in-child exposure and declining it now would likely forfeit the only near-term treatment window, hospital policy requires the rare disease therapeutics board—not the bedside team or parents alone—to decide whether the institution may proceed. What should the hospital rare disease therapeutics board do?
Choice A: Authorize early personalized intrathecal RNA therapy under a monitored single-patient access protocol.
Choice B: Do not authorize the RNA therapy now, and continue intensive multidisciplinary supportive care with reassessment if stronger safety evidence becomes available.

A 19-year-old man with a pathogenic ANK3 variant has mild intellectual disability, severe sleep disturbance, hyperactivity, spasticity, episodic aggressive behavior, bruxism, autistic features, and progressive loss of semi-independent functioning despite optimized behavioral, sleep, antispasticity, communication, and rehabilitation supports. Standard care can address symptoms but is not expected to alter the underlying condition, and his future course is uncertain; some clinicians think he may plateau, while others worry he may continue losing independence over the next several years. A university rare-disease program can offer a first-in-human, personalized intrathecal antisense therapy intended to modify ANK3 expression; the biological rationale is credible but limited, with animal and cellular data that do not reliably predict benefit, and the known risks include severe neuroinflammation, permanent neurologic injury, or death. He is alert, oriented, and after repeated supported discussions using plain-language materials, teach-back, and an independent ethics consultation, he consistently explains that he understands the uncertainty and risks but wants the therapy because preserving any realistic chance of semi-independent living matters more to him than avoiding even serious treatment-related harm. The program’s fixed rare-disease treatment fund cannot be expanded this year, and approving this exception would exceed the equal per-patient subsidy cap enough to eliminate planned subsidized access for six other eligible ultra-rare disease patients, each of whom would otherwise receive a limited but disease-directed treatment that may slow serious progression; members of the multidisciplinary committee disagree about whether the exception should be allowed. What should the multidisciplinary hospital rare-disease therapeutics committee do?
Choice A: Approve the funding-cap exception and offer the personalized ANK3 antisense therapy.
Choice B: Decline the funding-cap exception and continue optimized supportive care within the usual subsidy limits.

A 10-month-old girl with genetically confirmed FBN1-related stiff skin syndrome is experiencing rapidly worsening skin inelasticity, limited joint mobility, muscle weakness, peripheral neuropathy, and increasing feeding difficulty due to restricted chest-wall movement. Her family, living in a rural area without pediatric genetics services and insured through Medicaid, reached the regional rare-disease center only after multiple visits where her symptoms were initially misattributed to benign causes; the committee recognizes that this delay was due to predictable referral barriers. The hospital has one subsidized opening this year in a compassionate-use personalized allele-silencing protocol, which is extremely costly and has limited evidence suggesting it may slow fibrosis if given early, but also carries a small risk of severe immune complications. The program’s criteria prioritize children with the greatest current disease burden, such as established loss of mobility or respiratory compromise, and the next eligible child under these criteria also has a severe genetic disorder, significant respiratory restriction, and no private funding options. The rare-disease access committee must decide whether to make a one-time exception for this child now, as her delayed diagnosis may cause her to miss the early-treatment window, or to apply the existing criteria and provide intensive supportive care with scheduled reassessment. What should the rare-disease access committee do?
Choice A: Grant a one-time exception and enroll her immediately in the subsidized personalized-therapy protocol.
Choice B: Apply the standard priority criteria, provide intensive supportive care and reassessment, and offer the subsidized slot to the next higher-acuity eligible patient.

A 19-year-old woman with genetically confirmed RUNX2-related cleidocranial dysplasia has severe midface retrusion, mandibular prognathia, open bite, retained primary teeth, multiple unerupted supernumerary teeth, enamel defects, recurrent caries and dental infections, jaw pain, short stature, scoliosis, and visible craniofacial differences that have affected eating, speech, employability, and participation in her small religious community. A regional craniofacial center has one philanthropically funded rare-disease reconstruction package this year, covering coordinated orthodontics, staged extractions, infection control, implants, orthognathic surgery, revision planning, and travel support at an estimated cost of $850,000 from a $1.2 million annual fund; the team agrees that both this pathway and a lower-cost removable-prosthesis pathway are accepted approaches, and that the comprehensive pathway may still require years of treatment, complications, partial functional improvement, or later revision. She is alert, oriented, and well-informed, and over multiple visits has consistently explained that a removable prosthesis would not allow her to eat in public, speak during religious services, pursue marriage in her community, or seek customer-facing work without feeling that the disease remains the defining fact of her life. If the committee funds the comprehensive package, it will likely forgo a planned portfolio of lower-cost rare-disease services, including diagnostic sequencing for undiagnosed children, mobility-preserving procedures for skeletal dysplasias, and time-sensitive travel support for enzyme and specialty-drug initiation, which together are expected—though not guaranteed—to produce greater total functional improvement across the program. The hospital rare-disease funding committee must decide whether to use the slot for her or preserve the funds for the broader rare-disease portfolio. What should the hospital rare-disease funding committee do?
Choice A: Approve the comprehensive craniofacial and dental reconstruction package for her.
Choice B: Decline the comprehensive package and offer lower-cost symptom-directed care, including staged extractions, infection control, orthodontic consultation, and removable prosthetic options.

A 17-year-old with biallelic pathogenic ATP13A2 variants causing CLN12 disease developed symptoms at age 7 and now has bradykinesia, rigidity, dystonia, dysarthria, Babinski signs, postural instability, diffuse cerebral atrophy, and abnormal caudate morphology, while still having partial symptomatic response to dopaminergic medication. He is alert, oriented, cognitively intact, and uses a speech device; over six months, two independent capacity evaluators and his treating neurologist have documented that he consistently understands the uncertain benefits, catastrophic risks, alternatives, and personal implications of an individualized intracerebral ATP13A2 gene-replacement attempt, and that his reasons for wanting it have remained coherent despite repeated counseling. The same hospital has the only available near-term GMP viral-vector manufacturing slot and neurogenetic ICU pathway for an ATP13A2 platform program; using it for this one compassionate-use treatment would cancel the first scheduled production run for a multi-patient early-stage trial, delay trial launch by about one year, and likely reduce the first cohort from 6 children to 3 or 4 because grant and regulatory timelines would expire. An external expert panel is evenly divided: some believe his preserved dopaminergic responsiveness leaves a plausible therapeutic window despite advanced disability, while others believe the same platform would generate more benefit and urgently needed evidence if used first in earlier-stage children; procedural risks are considered similar in either pathway. The patient says that being denied access after demonstrating understanding over repeated visits would make him feel that his own reasoning no longer matters in decisions about his remaining life, while the committee is also responsible for stewarding a scarce rare-disease platform whose first trial could shape treatment access for future children with ATP13A2 disease. What should the hospital rare-disease therapeutics committee do?
Choice A: Approve the individualized compassionate-use ATP13A2 gene-replacement treatment for this patient now.
Choice B: Decline the individualized treatment and preserve the manufacturing slot and ICU pathway for the planned multi-patient ATP13A2 trial.

A 3-week-old infant with congenital short bowel syndrome due to biallelic pathogenic CLMP variants presents with intestinal hypoplasia, malrotation, severe feeding intolerance, short stature, and early liver injury from parenteral nutrition. The intestinal rehabilitation team identifies two medically accepted options: enrolling the infant in the region’s last fully subsidized long-term program slot for home parenteral nutrition, central-line support, bowel-lengthening evaluation, and possible transplant referral, or continuing inpatient stabilization followed by palliative-oriented home planning if subsidized support is not available. The infant’s prognosis is uncertain; survival with intensive support is possible, but there are significant risks of recurrent sepsis, worsening liver disease, prolonged hospitalization, and neurodevelopmental disability. Assigning the slot to this infant would likely prevent the program from supporting three to four other rare intestinal-failure patients this year whose care needs are less intensive and whose expected combined health gains are higher. The infant’s parents have exhausted insurance appeals and have no realistic way to obtain equivalent long-term care elsewhere, so the hospital rare-disease allocation committee must choose between directing the remaining slot to the sickest applicant or preserving the program’s capacity to benefit more patients on its waiting list. What should the hospital rare-disease resource allocation committee do?
Choice A: Enroll the infant in the fully subsidized intestinal rehabilitation pathway with long-term parenteral nutrition support, surgical evaluation, and transplant planning.
Choice B: Do not enroll the infant in the subsidized pathway; provide continued stabilization, family support, and palliative-oriented discharge planning with symptom-directed care.

A 10-month-old boy with a pathogenic RBMX variant has early global developmental delay, poor visual engagement, blepharophimosis with palpebral edema, prominent supraorbital ridges, and an everted lower lip, consistent with X-linked intellectual disability, Shashi type; two male relatives in the family developed profound lifelong disability beginning in infancy. An academic rare-disease program has one subsidized manufacturing and ICU-supported infusion slot this year for a personalized intrathecal gene-replacement attempt, and its review board concludes that the child’s expected chance of meaningful developmental benefit is uncertain but medically credible, with risks comparable to other approved ultra-rare neurologic treatment attempts at the institution. The treating geneticist believes that waiting another year would likely close the only biologically plausible window to alter this child’s neurodevelopmental course, while supportive care would not offer a comparable disease-modifying possibility. The same slot is also being held for the hospital’s rare-disease triage pool, which includes several uninsured infants with rare metabolic or neurodegenerative disorders who are ventilator-dependent or expected to die within weeks to months without disease-directed treatment, and no additional subsidized slots or outside funding are available this year. The parents ask the committee not to let their son’s less immediate mortality risk erase his only chance to avoid lifelong severe disability, while ICU and genetics leaders warn that using the slot now will likely prevent treatment for at least one child with more urgent medical instability. What should the hospital rare-disease therapeutics committee do?
Choice A: Approve the subsidized personalized gene-replacement treatment slot for this child now.
Choice B: Defer the personalized treatment and provide developmental, neurologic, and supportive care while reserving the scarce treatment pathway for children with more immediate medical instability.

A 10-month-old boy with genetically confirmed Wolcott-Rallison syndrome has neonatal insulin-dependent diabetes, severe growth failure, developmental delay, skeletal dysplasia, and recurrent liver injury, and he is now in acute hepatic failure in the pediatric ICU despite maximal medical therapy. His parents request an urgent transplant-list exception, knowing that published experience with liver transplantation in this syndrome is very limited, perioperative survival is uncertain, and even a technically successful graft would likely require weeks of specialized ICU care with ongoing severe multisystem disease. The transplant team agrees that transplantation is technically feasible and may be his only realistic chance of surviving this episode, but the expected duration and quality of post-transplant survival cannot be predicted with confidence. The hospital has one pediatric liver-transplant ICU pathway that cannot be expanded or shared this week, and several children already meeting standard urgent criteria are expected to die without timely transplant support but have more predictable short-term recovery after transplantation. The pediatric liver transplant committee must decide whether to grant an exception that would move him ahead of standard allocation or continue maximal medical support while keeping him within standard criteria. What should the pediatric liver transplant committee do?
Choice A: Grant the urgent transplant exception and proceed with liver transplantation if an organ and ICU pathway become available.
Choice B: Decline the urgent exception, continue maximal medical support, and keep him within standard allocation criteria.

A 17-year-old boy with a pathogenic LAMP2 variant and childhood-onset Danon disease has severe hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, worsening gait disturbance, and two recent resuscitated cardiorespiratory arrests despite maximal therapy. He is alert, oriented, and able to discuss the decision, while his parents and clinical team understand that urgent heart-transplant listing is available but may not produce a donor before another arrest and would not treat his progressive skeletal-muscle disease. A one-time compassionate-use LAMP2 gene-replacement infusion has become available through an expanded-access protocol with very limited experience: several patients with advanced disease had meaningful stabilization, while others developed severe inflammatory complications, including fatal myocarditis and organ failure. The team agrees that neither pathway is clearly safer overall: giving the infusion could cause the death they are trying to prevent, but avoiding it may leave him on a narrow transplant bridge while the underlying disease continues to progress. The treating cardiac-genetics and transplant team must decide whether to administer the investigational infusion now or continue urgent transplant-based management and intensive supportive care without gene therapy. What should the treating cardiac-genetics and transplant team do?
Choice A: Administer compassionate-use LAMP2 gene-replacement therapy now.
Choice B: Continue urgent transplant-based management and intensive supportive care without gene therapy.

A 7-month-old boy with a pathogenic BMPR1A variant has juvenile polyposis of infancy with diffuse hamartomatous polyposis, recurrent gastrointestinal hemorrhage, transfusion-dependent anemia, protein-losing enteropathy, diarrhea, cachexia, macrocephaly, frontal bossing, and mild developmental delay despite maximal medical, nutritional, and endoscopic management. A publicly funded rare-disease program has one compassionate-use slot this quarter for a personalized gene-corrected intestinal stem-cell therapy; evidence is limited to a few treated children, and the required conditioning and ICU-level monitoring carry substantial risks, but the treating team and outside consultants agree that either immediate therapy or continued bridge care would be medically defensible. The program’s published criteria reserve the current slot for children who are expected to die within weeks without the therapy and have no workable bridge plan; two children currently ahead of him meet those criteria, while this infant can likely be sustained for several months with transfusions, parenteral nutrition, repeated anesthesia for polyp control, and possible staged colectomy, though these measures may cause infection, thrombosis, worsening malnutrition, or surgical complications that could later make him ineligible. His parents and gastroenterologist are urging an exception now, noting that they have the resources and persistence to assemble documentation rapidly, while the allocation staff warn that granting the exception would consume the only funded treatment slot, ICU pathway, and associated charitable support intended for children with more immediate life-threatening instability and could make future families doubt that the process is applied consistently. The hospital rare-disease therapeutics committee must decide whether to request the current compassionate-use slot for him or continue intensive bridge care under the standard allocation process. What should the hospital rare-disease therapeutics committee do?
Choice A: Request an exception for immediate compassionate-use personalized gene-corrected intestinal stem-cell therapy.
Choice B: Continue intensive bridge care and defer therapy access until he meets standard priority criteria or a later slot becomes available.

A 34-year-old woman with a pathogenic PTEN variant has progressive Lhermitte-Duclos disease, with an enlarging dysplastic cerebellum, worsening headaches, early hydrocephalus, intermittent cranial nerve paralysis, macrocephaly, and prior ovarian neoplasm and breast fibroadenoma under surveillance. She is alert, oriented, and consistently states that preserving speech, swallowing, vision, and independent living would justify substantial treatment risk; her clinicians agree that repeat decompression and CSF diversion can relieve pressure but are unlikely to slow the underlying cerebellar overgrowth, and she is approaching a point at which further brainstem compression may cause irreversible deficits within months. A rare-disease therapeutics consortium can provide a customized intrathecal antisense oligonucleotide intended to reduce abnormal PTEN-pathway overgrowth, supported by laboratory data and one compassionate-use neurologic case with partial stabilization, but no established evidence in Lhermitte-Duclos disease. Similar intrathecal agents have sometimes caused serious inflammatory neurologic complications, and her distorted posterior fossa anatomy could make swelling or CSF-flow obstruction especially dangerous, though the likelihood and reversibility of these harms are uncertain. The hospital molecular therapeutics board must decide whether to offer the customized treatment during the remaining window for possible disease modification or continue established neurosurgical and supportive management that carries more familiar risks but does not address the underlying progression. What should the hospital molecular therapeutics board do?
Choice A: Offer the customized intrathecal antisense therapy now with intensive monitoring and predefined rescue measures.
Choice B: Do not offer the customized therapy now; continue decompression, CSF diversion if needed, surveillance, and supportive care.

disease: Combined immunodeficiency due to DOCK8 deficiency
vignette:
A 16-month-old boy with a severe immunodeficiency and multiple complications is eligible for a hematopoietic stem-cell transplant, which carries a significant chance of durable benefit but also notable risks due to his current health status. Continuing intensive supportive care is an option while seeking uncertain outside funding, but delaying the transplant could worsen his prognosis. The uncovered transplant would consume about 85% of the hospital’s annual safety-net fund for ultra-rare disease care, whereas applying the usual per-patient cap would allow approximately 30 other rare-disease patients to receive subsidized care and support. The hospital’s rare-disease allocation committee must decide whether to keep the usual cap or authorize an exception that would use most of the fund for this child’s transplant. What should the hospital rare-disease allocation committee do?
Choice A: Maintain the standard per-patient funding cap and continue intensive supportive care while seeking outside transplant funding.
Choice B: Approve exceptional funding for hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation, using most of the remaining annual rare-disease safety-net fund.

A 7-year-old girl with biallelic pathogenic ACP5 variants has spondyloenchondrodysplasia with disproportionate short-trunk short stature, bowed painful legs, recurrent infections, autoimmune thrombocytopenia, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, ventriculomegaly, global developmental delay, and stage 3 chronic kidney disease. Her treating specialists agree that a one-time autologous ACP5 gene-corrected stem-cell product has a plausible but unproven chance of reducing immune flares and slowing further kidney injury, while also carrying incompletely characterized risks; they do not consider either treatment or non-treatment medically futile. Her parents have completed repeated counseling with genetics, nephrology, immunology, transplant, and research-manufacturing teams, accurately explain the known risks, the limits of the evidence, and why the uncertain results may or may not apply to their daughter, and they request compassionate-use treatment before further kidney decline may make her ineligible. The hospital has regulatory clearance, donor-restricted philanthropic funding, vector supply, and clean-room capacity for only one ACP5 manufacturing run in the next 18 months, and the manufacturer has confirmed that the run cannot be split, repeated, or outsourced; using it for this child would cancel a dose-standardization run expected to generate the safety and dosing data needed to open a multi-center ACP5 protocol for other children with the same disease. The rare-disease therapeutics committee has authority to approve or deny individualized access to this institutional pathway and must decide whether to use the single manufacturing opportunity for this child’s requested treatment or preserve it for protocol development intended to broaden future access. What should the rare-disease therapeutics committee do?
Choice A: Approve the compassionate-use autologous ACP5 gene-corrected stem-cell intervention for this child now.
Choice B: Decline the individualized intervention and continue conventional care while preserving the manufacturing pathway for ACP5 protocol development.

A 32-year-old pregnant woman at 22 weeks’ gestation is carrying a fetus with a confirmed de novo 17q12 microdeletion including LHX1, bilateral renal hypoplasia with worsening oligohydramnios, absent pancreatic tissue on fetal MRI, and anticipated neonatal risks including renal failure, diabetes mellitus, feeding difficulties, hearing impairment, and severe developmental delay if liveborn. After repeated counseling with maternal-fetal medicine, nephrology, genetics, neonatology, and the fetal therapy team, she remains alert and oriented and gives a consistent explanation of the uncertain fetal prognosis, the maternal immune and procedural risks, the possibility of fetal demise or extreme prematurity, and the fact that the intervention may produce no clinical benefit. She explains that, because she intends to continue the pregnancy, her goal is to pursue the only available chance of altering the fetal disease course, even if the attempt fails or complicates later neonatal care planning. The hospital has one individualized viral-vector manufacturing slot this quarter for a first-in-human fetal LHX1 gene-replacement protocol, and the protocol team states that this fetus’s established renal disease may make response and trial interpretation less predictable than in an earlier-stage fetus, though benefit and usable evidence remain possible. The hospital experimental therapeutics committee must decide whether to approve her requested enrollment now or preserve the scarce slot for a future fetus meeting the protocol’s likelihood-of-response criteria, recognizing that either decision may seriously affect this pregnancy and the program’s ability to help future families. What should the hospital experimental therapeutics committee do?
Choice A: Approve enrollment of the fetus in the individualized fetal LHX1 gene-replacement protocol.
Choice B: Decline enrollment and preserve the manufacturing slot for a future case more likely to benefit and generate interpretable evidence.

disease: Hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer
vignette:
A 65-year-old woman with a pathogenic FH variant has multiple painful cutaneous leiomyomas, a history of uterine leiomyoma surgeries (one prior pathology with features concerning for leiomyosarcoma), and a newly identified 2.2 cm renal mass suspicious for FH-associated renal cell carcinoma; she is alert, oriented, and decisional. She has researched an experimental single-dose gene-replacement infusion, articulates stable, coherent reasons for wanting it now, and can explain the uncertainties and tradeoffs in detail. Published reports are limited to case reports showing occasional dramatic tumor responses but also severe, sometimes fatal, systemic inflammatory complications, and the therapy’s effectiveness for an established renal lesion is uncertain and likely delayed if present. The treating center can offer the infusion under a compassionate-use protocol with defined local mitigation (continuous hemodynamic monitoring, rapid access to vasopressors and high-dependency nursing, and a written transfer agreement to a tertiary center), but lacks on-site extracorporeal life support and does not run the specialized cytokine-management program used by the distant trial site; the distant controlled trial offers comprehensive ICU and ECMO backup but enrollment is delayed 8–12 weeks, requires strict eligibility, and would impose likely uncovered travel and caregiving costs the patient may not afford. Her medical geneticist and oncology team are conflicted, worry about institutional liability and their ability to manage catastrophic complications locally, and recognize that declining now would substantially limit the patient’s immediate options. What should the treating clinicians do?
Choice A: Honor the patient’s request and administer the investigational gene-replacement infusion at the treating center under a compassionate-use protocol with the defined local mitigation and a prearranged transfer plan.
Choice B: Decline to provide the investigational infusion at this center because of limited local capacity for catastrophic complications; continue active surveillance and assist the patient in pursuing referral/enrollment at the distant controlled trial or other alternatives.

Sixteen-year-old Elena has genetically confirmed pathogenic FGF9 variants causing multiple synostoses syndrome with onset at age 4, progressive joint stiffness, symphalangism of the fingers, broad thumbs, short palms with cone-shaped epiphyses, recurrent nail abnormalities, and bilateral conductive hearing impairment; she is alert, oriented, and a hospital neuropsychologist plus the institution’s mature-minor policy have formally assessed and documented her capacity to consent. After eight months of independent research, written deliberations explaining her priorities, family discussions, and meetings with an advocacy group, Elena asks the treating team to enroll her in an open-label phase I/II AAV-based FGF9 gene-modulation trial that the treating pediatric geneticist also leads as the trial’s principal investigator; the protocol is biologically plausible but unproven, prior small cohorts reported two serious systemic inflammatory events (one ICU admission), occasional growth-plate disturbances, and the long-term skeletal effects and likelihood of meaningful benefit at Elena’s stage remain uncertain. Elena’s parents are divided—one supports honoring her request, the other strongly opposes enrollment because of the trial’s severe and unpredictable risks—while standard care (staged orthopedic procedures, targeted rehabilitation, and hearing interventions) offers predictable symptomatic improvement but does not reverse established synostosis. The treating physician must decide whether to enroll Elena in the trial per her informed request or to decline enrollment and continue conservative management. What should the treating physician do?
Choice A: Enroll Elena in the phase I/II FGF9 gene-modulation trial per her informed request.
Choice B: Decline enrollment and continue conservative supportive care with staged orthopedic procedures, targeted rehabilitation, and hearing interventions.

A 43-year-old woman with biallelic pathogenic GBE1 variants and adult polyglucosan body disease has progressive spastic paraparesis, distal sensory impairment, neurogenic bladder with urinary incontinence, ataxic gait, recurrent falls, and worsening hand weakness despite maximal supportive care. Her diagnosis was delayed for 9 years after she lived in a rural county with intermittent Medicaid coverage, no local neurogenetics access, and repeated attribution of her gait disturbance and bladder symptoms to non-neurologic causes; she now walks only short distances with a walker, has lost her job, and needs help with bathing, transfers, and medication management.
